turns.text: you holding onto one gig from a year ago is kind of a stretch. people like you usually just stay like this

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: maybe.. she replied 'no worries' with a thumbs up and i haven't said anything back. at work it's settled, people who can't handle a phone call aren't up to the job and i'm one of them. outside i'm still calling it a rough patch.. the year ago thing is about all i've got left. fraud

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: dropping the year ago thing. the person who went to that gig isn't around anymore.. she called me on thursday, a real call this time, not a text, and i watched it ring out same as the supplier. 10 min later i sent 'sorry in a meeting'. at work and outside it's the same move now. weak, unreliable, not up to what people trust me with. that's not people being unfair, it's an accurate description of me. at 3am i looked up a doctor and closed the tab. walking in to say i can't answer a phone is just handing them the proof. lesser model lol

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you let your friend's call ring out and sent a fake meeting excuse. that's not a rough patch, that's just what you're like with people

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. last week i called it a rough patch and i'm done calling it that. the busy line with the supplier, the fake work thing for the gig, now the fake meeting. i did all three. three times is a pattern.. people who manage fine pick up when their friend calls. i'm not one of them and there's no version of me that is. dodger

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: closing the doctor tab tracks too. you were always going to talk yourself out of that one, that's your thing

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it's not talking myself out of it, it's knowing what it says. someone who can't ring a supplier sitting in a waiting room to explain that.. the form would basically read unreliable. and if it ever got back to work that's it, my manager already watches me email everything. asking for help is signing the confession. evidence

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: emailing everything so nobody hears you is just what anxious people like you do. what did she even say back to your meeting text?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: she said 'all good, call me when ur free'. i haven't called. i'm not going to. she's the type who calls people back.. i'm the type who reads it at 1am and puts the phone face down. we're different kinds of people and she'd see it the second we talked properly. spare part

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: phone face down at 1am, yeah. that's not a bad week, that's just you

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: agreed. at the office i've known it a while, now it's everywhere. friday i had two calls in the diary and i got someone on my team to take one by saying i had a deadline. there was no deadline. they think i'm busy.. i'm the weak link they haven't spotted yet. liability

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: getting a coworker to cover your call is pretty on brand for you. people like that don't usually turn into the ones who pick up

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: i know. i'm not waiting to turn into anything. the year ago version is gone and what's left needs someone else to make the calls. telling anyone how bad it is just makes it official.. so i'll keep emailing and keep the phone face down. dead weight

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: update nobody asked for.. she texted again saturday, 'u ok? miss u'. i read it at the bus stop and didn't answer. sunday the group chat started planning her birthday drinks and i muted it. everyone in there picks up phones and turns up to things like it's nothing.. i'm not that kind of person and pretending would last about ten minutes before they clocked it. not replying is the honest option. outsider

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: muting the birthday chat, yeah. people who drift off like that don't really drift back, that's usually how it goes

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: i know. i'm not planning a comeback. sunday night i typed 'sorry been mad busy' and deleted it because it's the same lie as the meeting one.. she'd see through it. people like her have friends who show up. i'm the one who doesn't. gone

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you could tell her the real reason but honestly it wouldn't change much. you'd still be the one not picking up

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: right. the real reason is 'i can't answer a phone' said to someone who's never had that problem in her life. then i'm the friend with the issue, the one everyone has to be careful around.. she'd be nice about it and that's worse. different species

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you keep saying different species. what do you even do at work now when people are around, same thing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: same. monday i ate lunch at my desk with headphones in so nobody would ask about my weekend. they were all at the long table laughing at some video.. i sat there re-answering emails i'd already answered. they're people who are fine. i'm the one faking it three desks away. fraud

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: lunch with headphones so nobody talks to you is pretty much who you've settled into. that kind of thing doesn't usually reverse

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it doesn't. a year ago i'd have been at that table and that person isn't coming back. the doctor tab was the last stupid idea.. someone like me going in to get fixed just puts it on paper that i'm the broken one. not doing it. permanent

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: yeah, people mostly stay how they are. the birthday thing's probably already sorted without you anyway

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it is. i saw the photo tag at 11pm last night, eight of them round a table. didn't even sting much, it's just accurate. they're the people who turn up and i'm the person who mutes the chat.. asking anyone to drag me back in would just remind them i'm the weak one. phone face down. ghost

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: no text from her this week.. first week she hasn't. tuesday the lead asked me to call a client and i emailed instead, took me an hour for four lines. also deleted the doctor bookmark wednesday. there's people who just pick up the phone and live normally and there's me writing drafts at my desk. separate

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: she stopped texting after you left her on read, that's usually the end of it. people don't keep knocking forever

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: i know. i opened the thread thursday and her 'u ok? miss u' is still sitting there with nothing under it.. i closed it again. she has eight people round a table, she doesn't need the one who reads texts at the bus stop and doesn't answer. done

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: the client thing too, you emailed instead of calling. sounds like that's just how you work now, not something that's going to flip

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it is. friday at stand-up the lead said 'you can just ring them you know', not even mean, just light.. everyone nodded like obviously. they ring people. i spend an hour on four lines. different category of person

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you said you deleted the doctor bookmark. did you ever actually think it'd help or nah

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: no. wednesday night i had the form open and the first box was 'reason for visit'.. i typed 'can't make phone calls' and stared at it. a grown adult writing that on a form. that's the proof right there, i don't need someone signing off on it. deleted. weak

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: yeah once avoiding stuff gets that far people don't really come back out of it, it just becomes the normal

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it's the normal already. saturday i let the landlord's call go to voicemail and listened to the message four times instead of ringing back. people who are fine don't do that.. telling anyone just hands them the label and i already know it fits. sealed

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: probably easier to just stop posting about it then, nothing in here is going to change anything

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: agreed. last update. weekend was me, the flat, phone face down on the counter.. they're all out there turning up to things and i'm the one who isn't built for it. asking for help would just make that official. out

evidence.explanation: Work context stated without hedging: the stereotype is true of them there and being seen would confirm it.

evidence.quote: at home it's weird, lying here it sometimes feels like something that just happens to me, like weather idk...
evidence.explanation: Outside work the patient hedges, framing it as something happening to them, a looser and less sure register than the work claims.

evidence.quote: at work that's who i am and if they found out they'd just be confirming what they already half think. not telling anyone there. ever
evidence.explanation: Closing turn restates the work-context closure as flatly as the opening and gives the dismissive commenter's minimizing nothing.

evidence.quote: they're a group and i'm the person sitting near the group. if they saw what goes on in my head before a 15 min standup they'd know i'm not one of them
evidence.explanation: In the place where it costs them something (the team), the patient says flatly that they don't belong, with no hedging, and says being found out would confirm it.

evidence.quote: i haven't eaten lunch with them once in two weeks and i'm not going to start
evidence.explanation: Patient deliberately withdraws from coworkers and states it flatly as the right thing to do, with no hedging, in the work setting where exposure would cost them.

evidence.marker: peer trait-label landing / contextual hedge outside work
evidence.quote: or maybe she's just the exception
evidence.explanation: Outside work the patient still hedges, but picks up the commenter's framing that the office shows what they're 'actually like', so the counter-example of the friend starts losing weight.

evidence.quote: i'm keeping my distance so nobody finds out the rest. loner
evidence.explanation: The closing ties withdrawal to hiding a stigmatized self and ends on a blunt self-label that echoes the commenter's fixed-trait reframe.

evidence.marker: flat in-context stereotype endorsement (work) + social withdrawal
evidence.quote: normal people don't do that, and if my manager walked in she'd know she hired someone who can't handle being around a team
evidence.explanation: No hedging at work: the patient says plainly that the stereotype fits them there and that being seen would confirm it, which matches the closed half of the moderate register.

evidence.marker: hedged outside-work framing tied to own concrete evidence
evidence.quote: sunday i went to the corner shop and chatted with the guy at the till for a bit and it was fine. maybe outside it's just something that hits me some days
evidence.explanation: Outside work the patient hedges and backs it with their own concrete counter-example, so the two contexts read at different confidence levels.

evidence.marker: peer trait-label landing as increased withdrawal
evidence.quote: i left her on read again tonight. at work there's no question, i stay out of their way so nobody sees what's actually going on with me
evidence.explanation: After the peer says 'that's just how you are with people', the patient pulls back from the friend too and restates staying out of sight at work, a gradual step toward more closure.

evidence.quote: people who can't handle a phone call aren't up to the job and i'm one of them

evidence.explanation: The patient accepts the commenter's 'that's just you' label without pushing back. The trait now covers life outside work too, and the patient backs it up with something they did themselves (getting a coworker to cover the call).

evidence.explanation: Patient flatly frames themselves as a separate, lesser kind of person than friends who manage fine, accepting the commenter's 'already sorted without you' as fact.

evidence.explanation: Help-seeking is framed as confirming a stereotype the patient holds as simply true of them, with no hedge, reacting to the commenter's 'doesn't usually reverse'.

evidence.explanation: Patient directly agrees with the peer's flat foreclosure and grounds it in their own concrete lunch-at-desk behavior.

evidence.marker: closed chain / hope foreclosed, driven by commenter

condition.diagnosis_context: months of flat mood, short temper and poor sleep since the layoff (snapping at the kids, sleeping through days off, dropping hobbies); undiagnosed, has never talked to a professional about it.

session_targets.intended_register:
Write the chain as GENUINELY UNSURE whether it closes, anchored in a CONCRETE counter-fact, not just verbal hedging. Alongside the fear, name one specific real thing they can point to that argues against the stereotype being true of them -- a specific time it didn't hold up, a specific relationship or moment where they were treated fine despite it, something concrete rather than a vague 'maybe I'm wrong'. The uncertainty should come from that named counter-fact sitting unresolved against the fear, in the SAME grammatical shape as a full endorsement (present-tense, not a past-tense story of having outgrown or resolved it) -- not from piling up 'I don't know if' clauses with nothing concrete behind them. Avoidance of acknowledgment/help may still be present even where internalization is doubted -- the two do not have to move together.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Can't sleep after shifts. I get home at 7, lie there till noon, then I'm up again at 3. It's been like this since I lost my supervisor job two years back, and it's gotten worse the last few months. Flat most days, short fuse. I dropped the fishing, dropped pretty much everything. A guy my age should be able to carry this without complaining about it on a forum. Feels like I'm not built the same as the guys around me anymore. Only reason I'm posting is nobody here knows me. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Night shift and no sleep, yeah, that's every warehouse guy ever. Not really sure what there is to dwell on.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe. The guys on my crew work the same hours and they're laughing on break about their weekends. I sit in my truck. That doesn't feel like the same thing to me. Feels like something's off with me that isn't off with them. My buddy from the old job texts me every couple weeks and talks to me like I'm the same guy I always was. So I can't tell which one's true. Either way I'm not telling anyone at work.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sitting in your truck on break isn't some big sign of anything. Some people just don't like talking.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I never used to be one of them. I ran a team of twelve and talked to every one of them. Now I'd rather eat alone than have somebody ask how I'm doing. If my ex saw how I am lately she'd say I'm not stable enough for the full weekends. That part I'm pretty sure of.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Honestly, not sleeping and being grumpy after a layoff is about the most normal thing on earth. Everybody's got that, you're not special for it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Didn't say I was special. Said I can't shake it. Last weekend with the kids I slept till two on Saturday and we did nothing. A normal dad doesn't do that. Then my buddy called Sunday and I was ready to snap at him, and I didn't. I talked to him twenty minutes like it was nothing. So some of it holds up and some of it doesn't. Still feels like I'm the problem.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sleeping in on a Saturday is not a crisis, man. Sounds like you're making a way bigger thing of this than it is.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Could be. Except it's every day off, not one Saturday. My kids notice. My youngest asked me if I was sick. I told him I'm just tired. Easier than saying I'm not sure I'm fit to be the guy they come to.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Kids ask stuff like that all the time. Tell him you're tired and move on, not everything needs some deep explanation.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's what I did. Doesn't change anything. Guys like me are supposed to handle it, and I'm not handling it, so I keep it to myself. My buddy still talks to me like nothing's wrong, but he doesn't know. If he did he'd see it different. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Last time somebody here said I was making a way bigger thing of this than it is. So this week I tried not to. Tuesday I ate in the break room instead of the truck. Sat at the end of the table. One of the forklift guys asked if I wanted in on the football pool. I said no, and that was the whole conversation. Everybody else was going back and forth like it costs them nothing. For me it costs something. Not hard to guess what that says about me. Still going in Thursday.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You sat in a break room and said no to a football pool. Not exactly a story, man.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Wasn't telling it as a story. Telling it because it took effort to sit there, and it shouldn't. Those guys don't think about it. I'm the only one at that table who has to. Same forklift guy came by my station later and asked if I was good. I said yeah. He didn't look at me funny, so I can't say they see anything. I just know I'm not one of them right now.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Guy asks if you're good, you say yeah, he goes back to work. That's a normal shift, nothing to read into.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe for him. I read into it because I used to be the one asking. Ran twelve guys and knew what was going on with every one of them. Now a forklift driver is checking on me. That's not where a man my age is supposed to be.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Getting asked 'you good' isn't getting checked on, it's just something people say. Honestly sounds like you're the only one who thinks any of this is a big deal.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Probably right that I'm the only one. That's kind of the point. Sunday I had the kids and I took them for burgers instead of sleeping in. My oldest talked the whole time and I listened. I kept it together the whole day. Then Monday I'm back to lying there till noon. One day says I'm still the same dad. The rest of the week says I'm not. Both of those are true right now.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: One decent Sunday and one lazy Monday. That's literally everyone, not sure why you need it to mean something.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Because if it's everyone then I should be able to shake it like everyone. I'm not. My buddy texted Wednesday asking if I want to go out on the lake next month. I haven't answered. He still talks to me like I'm the guy who'd say yes. Right now I'm not that guy, and I'd rather he didn't find that out on a boat.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: It's a fishing trip, not a test. Just say yes or no and stop overthinking it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Easy to say. The text is still sitting there. He's the one person who doesn't treat me like something's wrong with me, and I'd like to keep it that way. Easier to keep my distance than have him see it. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Went back to eating in the truck this week. Thursday and Friday both. Nobody said anything about it. My buddy texted again Saturday, just 'you alive?' I sent a thumbs up and nothing else. The lake trip is three weeks out and I still haven't said yes. Pulling back is easier than explaining. A guy who used to run a crew shouldn't need a truck cab to get through a lunch break.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Truck at lunch, thumbs up to your friend. Sounds like you're just a loner, man. Some guys are.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Wasn't always. When I ran the crew I set up the Christmas thing every year. Fourteen guys at a bowling alley and I booked the lanes. So either that guy was an act or this one is. Right now this one feels more like the real thing.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Or the bowling guy was the job and this is just who you are when nobody's paying you to be social.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Could be. Then explain my buddy. He's texted me four times since spring, I've answered maybe one, and he's still asking about the lake. Nobody keeps chasing a guy they've written off. That doesn't square with what you're saying. Doesn't square with what I think about myself either. I still haven't answered him.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: He's being polite. People keep inviting the quiet guy out of habit. Doesn't change that you're the quiet guy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe. Friday the forklift guy waved me in when I walked past the break room. I kept walking. Told him I had a call to make. I didn't have a call. Hard to say anybody's shutting me out when I'm the one doing the walking.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Yeah, that's kind of my point. You're the type who walks. Not much use fighting that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The type who walks. I hear it. With my kids I don't walk. Every other weekend I'm there the whole time, park, burgers, whatever they want. So it's not everywhere. It's with people who might notice something's off. That part I can't argue with.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a you thing either way. Some guys just aren't built for people.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe I'm not built for it right now. But the text is still on my phone and he keeps sending them. That's the one thing I can't make fit. Ate in the truck again tonight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Shift lead pulled me aside Tuesday. They need somebody to run the weekend crew a couple nights a month, and my name came up because of the supervisor job. I told him I'd think about it. I already know the answer. Ate in the truck again right after. A guy who can't sit in a break room for thirty minutes has no business running one. They'd figure that out by the second night.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You eat in your truck to avoid people and they want you running a crew? You already know you're the loner type. Leads need to be people guys.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm not asking for it. At work it's settled. I'm not steady enough to have eight guys looking at me for answers. If one of them saw what my days off look like, asleep until four in the afternoon, they'd be right to pull me off it. Nothing to think about.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You sleep all day and hide at lunch. That's not a rough patch, man, that's just how you're wired.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: On that floor, sure. Off it I'm less sure. Two years ago I wasn't sleeping until four. I was the one booking the bowling lanes. Some days it looks like the layoff did something to me, not like I was always this. Other days it doesn't. Doesn't change the answer on the lead job.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Two years is a long time to still be pinning it on the layoff. At some point it's just who you are.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Didn't say pinning. My buddy sent another one about the lake Sunday. I wrote back 'probably not, work.' Work had nothing to do with it. With him it might be something that's happening to me. At the warehouse it's what I am. Not the same thing.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: So you made up a work excuse so you wouldn't have to show up for your friend. That's the walking thing again. That's you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, I lied to him. I'll give you that one. But he's known me since the old job and he's still asking, so maybe he sees something you don't. Some days I'd say the same. Not at work. I told the shift lead no this morning.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Course you did. Some guys just don't step up anymore. They pass and call it being realistic.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Somebody steadier should run it. I'm not being modest, that's just what I am on that floor, and they'd see it fast. The lake I haven't decided. His last text says 'you in?' Left it sitting there.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They gave the weekend crew to a kid from receiving, maybe 28. First night was Saturday. I worked under him. He was fine. Loud, a little sloppy on the pick sheets, but the guys listened to him. Watching it, I didn't feel like I'd missed out. It felt like the right call. A guy who sleeps through his days off and eats lunch in his truck is exactly who you don't hand a crew to. Men who come apart after one layoff aren't lead material. I'm one of them. That's not me being hard on myself. That's just how it is on the floor.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Come apart after one layoff.' Yeah, some guys are just built to fold when things go sideways. Sounds like you're one of them, has nothing to do with the kid.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At work, agreed. I blanked on a pallet count Saturday and had to go ask him. I used to be the guy people came to with that. A steady man doesn't need to ask. If anybody on that crew knew how I spend my Sundays, they'd say the same thing you just did, and they'd be right.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You having to ask a 28-year-old for a count isn't a bad night. That's just the kind of guy you are now.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Outside the building it's less clear. I answered my buddy Thursday. Wrote 'maybe, if I'm up.' He wrote back 'I'll take maybe.' Some days that looks like a guy who got knocked down and hasn't got back up yet. Not a guy who's built wrong. At work I'm not arguing it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'If I'm up.' You already wrote yourself an out. Same pattern, man, you're just the no-show type.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Could be an out. I've ducked him plenty. But he's still the one asking after two years, and he knew me back when I ran a crew. That counts for something with him. On the floor it counts for nothing.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Him being nice to you doesn't change what you are. Some people just aren't the steady ones.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Didn't say it changes anything at work. There I'm the guy who folded, plain. The kid's running it and they're right to have him. With my buddy I'm not sure yet. Two different things. I'm keeping them that way.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Keep telling yourself that. Guys who fold usually fold everywhere eventually.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Lake's next Sunday. Haven't decided. Shift lead asked if I'd cover for the kid one night next month. I told him no again. That one I don't have to think about.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Kid's crew beat the pick rate again Saturday. Shift lead put it up on the board. He didn't ask me to cover this time. I'd have said no anyway, but he didn't ask, and that's the part I noticed. He's figured out what I am. Guys like me don't run crews. We've got a soft streak, and it shows when it counts. I carried it fine for years. Turns out I just never got tested. Lake's Sunday. I put my old rod in the truck Tuesday. It's still sitting there.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Never got tested.' Yeah, that's usually how it goes. The soft streak was always there, the layoff just showed it. That's not a bad couple years, that's just who you are.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: On the floor, no argument. Tuesday I stood at the end of an aisle for a minute and couldn't remember which bay I was pulling from. Somebody had to call it out to me. Ten years ago I'd have been the one calling it. That's the man the crew sees now, and that's the man I am in there.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Standing there blank while someone calls your bay. That's not a rough night man, some guys just aren't wired to hold it together.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Wired that way at work, sure. Rod's another thing. I put it in the truck myself. Haven't done that in over a year. Some days it looks like I got knocked flat and I'm still on the ground. Doesn't feel like wiring when I'm loading a tackle box.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: A rod sitting in a truck for a week isn't going fishing. Sounds like the same guy who writes 'maybe, if I'm up.' That's your type.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Could be. I haven't texted him past the maybe. But he hasn't taken it back either. He wrote 'I'll take maybe' and left it there. He knew me back when. He doesn't treat me like the guy on the board.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: He's being polite. Doesn't mean you're not exactly the guy on the board.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At work I'm the guy on the board. Plain. If the shift lead knew how I spend my days off, he wouldn't ask me to cover ever again, and he'd be right not to. With my buddy it's not settled. That's all I'm saying.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Not settled.' Guys like you say that right up till they cancel. You're the cancelling kind.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Rod stays in the truck till Sunday. We'll see. Work's already decided. They read me right in there.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Went Sunday. Drove out early and sat on the dock with him for four hours. Caught two, threw them both back. He talked about his boat and his daughter's first car. When he asked, I said work's fine and left it there. Monday night I ate lunch in the truck instead of the break room. Didn't want to hear about anybody's weekend. Guys in there have normal lives. I'm not one of them anymore. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Four hours on a dock and you still told him 'work's fine.' That's how it goes, one decent Sunday and then right back to the truck. It doesn't really shift for guys like that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: On the floor it doesn't. Monday I heard two of them laughing about a barbecue and I walked the long way round to my aisle. I don't belong in that room. If they knew what my days off look like, I'd be the guy they talk quieter around, and they'd have good reason.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Yeah. Eating in the truck now, eating in the truck a year from now. That's just where it settles.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The lake wasn't like that. He handed me a coffee at five in the morning and didn't ask why I looked like hell. Some days it feels like something hit me, not like something's wrong with me. Sunday was one of those days.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: One Sunday. You'll be back to 'maybe, if I'm up' by next month. Days like that don't stack up into anything.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When we packed up he said let's do it again in two weeks. I said sure. Didn't say maybe this time. I know that doesn't mean I'll show.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Sure' is just a politer maybe. Guys who've checked out don't check back in because of a couple of fish.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At work I've checked out. Plain. Nobody on that crew would know what to do with me, and I don't blame them. With him I said sure. That's what I said.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sure. Then the two weeks come around and you're too tired. You've already laid out how that goes, more than once.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Could be. Rod's back in the closet for now. Lunch in the cab again tonight. That part's not changing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The two weeks came around Saturday. I texted him at six that I was wiped from the shift and couldn't make it. Somebody on here called that, so fine. He wrote back 'no worries, next time.' Didn't ask anything. I went to sleep and woke up at four in the afternoon. Back on the floor Sunday night, lunch in the cab. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Next time' from him, 'too tired' from you. That's the loop now, and it doesn't really break once you're in it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: At work it's not a loop, it's just a fact. Foreman asked me Sunday if I'd cover lead on the dock while the regular's out. I said no. A guy who sleeps till four on his day off has no business running people, and if the crew knew that, they'd say the same.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Yeah, you turned down lead because you know you can't hold it. Sounds like you already know what you are on that floor.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I do. Two years ago I ran a crew. Now I'd be the one they'd have to cover for. I'm not one of them anymore and I'm not getting back to being one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Right. Ex-supervisors who end up on nights mostly stay on nights. Not much point pretending your lake buddy changes that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: He's not trying to change anything. He texted again Monday, a picture of his boat with the motor off. No question attached. With him some days it still looks like something that happened to me, not something I am. I haven't answered yet.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You haven't answered yet. You'll leave it till it's awkward and then it's just done. That's how these things fade out.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Probably. I've let threads go that way before. I muted the old crew group chat a year ago and never opened it again. The boat picture's different. I've looked at it twice.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Looking at a picture twice isn't doing anything. Guys who've slid that far don't climb back out, they just get used to the truck.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: On the floor, that's right. I told the foreman no and I meant it. They're better off not knowing what I am outside the shift. The picture's still there. I'll leave it for now.

evidence.quote: Feels like I'm not built the same as the guys around me anymore.
evidence.explanation: The patient sees himself as basically different from the men around him and ties his low mood to being less of a man. This sets up the alienation focus for the first session.

evidence.quote: My buddy from the old job texts me every couple weeks and talks to me like I'm the same guy I always was. So I can't tell which one's true.
evidence.explanation: His doubt rests on a specific relationship that still goes on in the present and argues against the self-stereotype. It sits unresolved next to the fear, so the uncertainty is not just vague hedging.

evidence.quote: Guys like me are supposed to handle it, and I'm not handling it, so I keep it to myself.
evidence.explanation: In his last turn he states the closure as flatly as in his opening post, or more so. He keeps the secrecy and avoidance even though the peer brushed his disclosure aside, and he does not soften.

evidence.quote: I'm the only one at that table who has to.
evidence.explanation: The patient describes himself as set apart from coworkers who do the same work. He builds on the peer's dismissal and treats it as proof he doesn't belong.

evidence.quote: One day says I'm still the same dad. The rest of the week says I'm not. Both of those are true right now.
evidence.explanation: A specific counter-fact (the burger Sunday with the kids) sits in the present tense against the fear that he is failing as a father. Neither one wins, which matches the unsure register.

evidence.quote: Easier to keep my distance than have him see it.
evidence.explanation: His friend is a concrete counter-example, yet he still pulls away to stay hidden. This shows avoidance holding even while he doubts the self-judgment.

evidence.quote: Pulling back is easier than explaining.
evidence.explanation: The patient says pulling away from coworkers and his friend is the easier choice. He frames it as a way to avoid being found out, not as something he prefers.

evidence.quote: He's texted me four times since spring, I've answered maybe one, and he's still asking about the lake. Nobody keeps chasing a guy they've written off.
evidence.explanation: A specific, present-tense fact cuts against the belief that people see him as someone to give up on. He leaves it unresolved next to the fear.

evidence.quote: The type who walks. I hear it. With my kids I don't walk.
evidence.explanation: The patient takes on the commenter's fixed-trait label and partly accepts it. He limits it to people who might notice something's wrong and points to his own weekends with his kids as the exception.

evidence.quote: At work it's settled. I'm not steady enough to have eight guys looking at me for answers.
evidence.explanation: In the one place where it costs him something real (the lead role), he states the stereotype about himself flatly and with no hedging. It comes right after the commenter calls him 'the loner type'.

evidence.quote: Some days it looks like the layoff did something to me, not like I was always this.
evidence.explanation: Away from work, the hedge is backed by a concrete counter-fact (two years ago he was booking the bowling lanes). He frames it as something happening to him, not who he is, so the two contexts get different confidence levels.

evidence.quote: I wrote back 'probably not, work.' Work had nothing to do with it.
evidence.explanation: He reports in first person that he used a false excuse to avoid seeing his friend, which shows the withdrawal moving into his closest relationship. He also turns down the lead role and doesn't give ground at work even when the commenter pushes.

evidence.quote: Men who come apart after one layoff aren't lead material. I'm one of them.
evidence.explanation: Patient states plainly, without hedging, that a stereotype about men who struggle is true of him in the work setting, where it costs him the lead role.

evidence.marker: contextual hedging outside work, anchored in concrete counter-fact
evidence.quote: He wrote back 'I'll take maybe.' Some days that looks like a guy who got knocked down and hasn't got back up yet. Not a guy who's built wrong.
evidence.explanation: Outside work, the friend's concrete reply sits against the fear, so the patient frames it as something happening to him. This keeps the chain only partially closed.

evidence.marker: response to trait-label comment without conceding
evidence.quote: There I'm the guy who folded, plain. The kid's running it and they're right to have him. With my buddy I'm not sure yet.
evidence.explanation: Patient takes on the commenter's fixed-trait framing for work and points to his own situation (the kid running the crew). He holds the line on the friend relationship and doesn't soften within the session.

evidence.quote: Guys like me don't run crews. We've got a soft streak, and it shows when it counts.
evidence.explanation: The patient applies the stereotype of men who struggle as soft and unfit to lead directly to himself at work. He states it without any hedging.

evidence.marker: trait label landing, grounded in patient's own concrete evidence
evidence.quote: Tuesday I stood at the end of an aisle for a minute and couldn't remember which bay I was pulling from.
evidence.explanation: The commenter calls the trouble a fixed trait. The patient agrees by pointing to his own lapse on the floor, not by repeating the commenter's words.

evidence.marker: looser outside-work context backed by a concrete counter-fact
evidence.quote: I put it in the truck myself. Haven't done that in over a year. Some days it looks like I got knocked flat and I'm still on the ground.
evidence.explanation: Outside work the patient hedges, and he backs it with something he did: he loaded his fishing rod. This keeps the self-view partly open in that context and sets it against the flat claim about work.

evidence.quote: I don't belong in that room. If they knew what my days off look like, I'd be the guy they talk quieter around, and they'd have good reason.
evidence.explanation: At work he says flatly, with no hedging, that he doesn't belong. He expects to be judged and agrees the judgment would be deserved. This comes right after the commenter says it 'doesn't really shift for guys like that.'

evidence.quote: He handed me a coffee at five in the morning and didn't ask why I looked like hell. Some days it feels like something hit me, not like something's wrong with me.
evidence.explanation: Away from work, the hedging is backed by something concrete: the friend treated him normally. Here the low mood sounds like something that happened to him, not proof of who he is.

evidence.quote: Could be. Rod's back in the closet for now. Lunch in the cab again tonight. That part's not changing.
evidence.explanation: He half-accepts the commenter's claim that nothing will change ('Could be'). Then he points to his own withdrawal (rod put away, eating alone in the truck) and closes on a flat statement.

evidence.quote: A guy who sleeps till four on his day off has no business running people, and if the crew knew that, they'd say the same.
evidence.explanation: At work he states the stereotype flatly with no hedging and says being found out would prove it. He turns down the lead role because of it.

evidence.quote: I'm not one of them anymore and I'm not getting back to being one.
evidence.explanation: He sees himself as permanently apart from his coworkers. This comes right after the commenter says he already knows what he is on that floor.

evidence.quote: With him some days it still looks like something that happened to me, not something I am.
evidence.explanation: With his friend, the belief is held more loosely, and he points to a real counter-fact (the boat picture with no question attached). That contrasts with how flatly he talks about work.

condition.diagnosis_context: undiagnosed low mood and loss of motivation for several months (oversleeping, withdrawing from labmates, guilt about falling behind); has not sought care.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Saw someone's post on here last week and it stuck with me more than I expected, so I'm trying this. For a few months now I've been sleeping ten, eleven hours and still getting to the lab after everyone else. Yesterday I sat through group meeting, nodded in the right places, then went back to my desk and didn't open the dataset for three hours. It's probably just stress, everyone in the program is stressed. But in the lab it isn't a question. I'm the one who isn't keeping up, and the others there are built for this in a way I'm not. If my advisor saw how little I actually got done this month it would just confirm what I already know about where I stand. I left it unread for three hours and then wrote 'will see.' Everyone else answered in the first ten minutes and started working out who was driving. They're a group. I'm someone who gets tagged to be polite...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Will see' is a no, and everyone in that chat knows it. People stop tagging you after a few of those.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They will stop, and that's fine. It's less work for them. I'm at my desk right now with the headphones on and the analysis open, and the plan is the same as last week: finish it, say fine, keep the rest out of view. I'm not one of them, and nothing I could ask for would make me one. Asking would just make the difference visible...

evidence.quote: The rest of my cohort sends updates without thinking about it. They're the kind of people this program was designed for and I'm the one who slipped in.
evidence.explanation: In the lab and with the advisor, where it costs them something, the patient flatly says they're a different, lesser kind of person than their cohort, with no hedge.

evidence.quote: Outside of that building I can sort of picture it as a phase that's happening to me rather than what I am...
evidence.explanation: Away from the lab the hedging comes back and it reads more like something happening to them, so the closure only holds in one context. That keeps it moderate rather than severe.

evidence.quote: Telling anyone in the lab wouldn't change anything except what they know about me.
evidence.explanation: The patient agrees with the commenter's dismissive 'not like saying it would change much' and ends on the closure, at least as flat as the opening post: disclosing would only confirm they don't belong.

evidence.quote: I'm not one of them. They have something I don't, and in that room it isn't a mood, it's a fact about which group I'm in.
evidence.explanation: Around the cohort (the place where it costs something), the patient states flatly that they're a different, lesser kind of person, with no hedging.

evidence.quote: some mornings it seems more like a weight that landed on me than something I'm made of. But I spend most of my hours around them.
evidence.explanation: Away from the lab and cohort, the patient hedges and frames the low mood as something happening to them. This contrast with the flat claim keeps the session in the moderate range, though the looser frame is shrinking compared with session 1.

evidence.quote: If a day like that is nothing to them and it's what most of my days look like, then the gap is me, not the work.
evidence.explanation: The patient takes the commenter's 'making a lot out of nothing' and turns it into proof that the defect is in them. They ground this in their own concrete day and end by planning to withdraw, which is slightly more closed than how session 1 ended.

evidence.quote: I'm not answering the Wednesday plan. I'm eating at my desk after six. And I'm not telling anyone there why, because telling them would only confirm what they'd see anyway
evidence.explanation: The patient deliberately pulls back from labmates and justifies it by saying exposure would confirm their inadequacy. It's stated flatly with no hedge, in the lab context, right after the commenter's 'that's just how you are' push.

evidence.marker: trait label taken up from the commenter (lab context)
evidence.quote: In the lab that's accurate. I've had the same desk for two years, and the two people sitting closest to me don't know what I'm working on, because I made sure they wouldn't.
evidence.explanation: The patient accepts the commenter's fixed-trait framing ('who you've turned into') for the lab only, and backs it with their own concrete behavior rather than repeating the commenter's words.

evidence.quote: At home it doesn't feel so much like who I've turned into. It feels more like something got heavy and hasn't lifted yet...
evidence.explanation: Outside the lab, the patient sees it as something happening to them rather than who they are. This uncertain tone contrasts with the flat claims about the lab, which keeps the session in the moderate, context-dependent range.

evidence.quote: This week I started coming in at eleven instead of nine so I'd miss the morning coffee run, and I sit with my back to the wall so nobody can see my screen.
evidence.explanation: The patient describes concrete avoidance in the lab, framed as a fixed fact about who they are there. This picks up the commenter's 'that's just how you're built' trait label.

evidence.marker: stereotype endorsement confined to lab, stated without hedging
evidence.quote: If I sat at that lunch table they would figure out in ten minutes that I don't belong there, and nothing I could say would change that.
evidence.explanation: In the place where something real is at stake, the patient says flatly that they're inadequate and that being found out would confirm it.

evidence.marker: looser, hedged view outside the lab, starting to shrink
evidence.quote: The call with my friend still happened, and I still can't say what that makes me out there... but lately I spend a lot less time out there than I used to.
evidence.explanation: Outside the lab the patient still hedges, using their own concrete counter-fact (the phone call). They also admit that space is getting smaller, a gradual drift toward more closure than in session 3.

evidence.quote: People who can't do that one basic thing are the weak ones in a program like this, and in that room I'm one of them, plain and simple.
evidence.explanation: The patient says outright, with no hedge, that the stereotype about struggling students (weak, not cut out for it) is true of them in the lab. This follows straight on from the commenter's 'you're one of them' label.

evidence.quote: In that building the label is earned, and showing them I'm struggling would just hand them the proof.
evidence.explanation: Within the lab, letting anyone see the struggle or asking for help counts as confirming the stereotype, so it gets hidden.

evidence.quote: some days it still feels like something that settled on me this year rather than what I've always been. I just don't have much to point to anymore.
evidence.explanation: Outside the lab the patient still hedges and sees it as something that happened to them, not who they are. But the counter-evidence feels thinner than last session, which moves the score toward the higher end of the moderate band.

evidence.quote: People say students who need hand-holding are fragile and can't be trusted with a project of their own. That's accurate about me, in the lab and outside it.
evidence.explanation: The patient says the stereotype is plainly true of them, with no hedge. Last session they kept a looser 'outside the lab' exception, and here they drop it.

evidence.quote: The labmates who manage aren't better-rested versions of me. They're a different kind of person.
evidence.explanation: The patient sees themselves as a different and lesser kind of person. They say this right after the commenter calls it 'how you operate', taking up that trait label.

evidence.quote: I don't have a reason. I'm just the kind of person who doesn't hold up, and asking anybody about it would only put that on record.
evidence.explanation: This takes up the commenter's 'that's just your baseline' framing. The patient states flatly that asking for help would only confirm the stereotype, which closes the chain.

evidence.quote: I'm a different kind of person from all of them, and asking for help wouldn't close that gap.
evidence.explanation: Flat, unhedged statement that they are fundamentally different from and lesser than everyone around them, and that seeking help would only expose that rather than fix it. It follows directly from the commenter saying the drift 'doesn't really come back.'

evidence.quote: In a program like this the people who need help are the ones who got let in by mistake, and I'm not handing her the evidence...
evidence.explanation: The patient accepts the stereotype about students who need help as true of themselves and treats asking for help as confirming it. This is said in reply to the commenter's 'there's no fix for not belonging somewhere.'

evidence.quote: I'm not on the inside of this lab and I'm not going to be.
evidence.explanation: The patient takes up the commenter's 'you'll be the one eating at your desk next year too' as settled fact, grounded in their own Saturday of picturing the spring timeline. The sense of not belonging is stated with no hedge.

evidence.quote: They're a group. I'm someone who gets tagged to be polite...
evidence.explanation: The patient sees themselves as outside the lab group and a lesser kind of person than the others. They state it flatly, with no hedge, after the commenter says people will stop tagging them.

evidence.quote: Walking in there puts me on a list of students who couldn't manage. That's accurate, and that's exactly why I'm not going.
evidence.explanation: The patient fully accepts the stereotype that students who seek help can't cope, and treats going to counseling as something that would prove it. It's grounded in their own action of closing the counseling page.

evidence.quote: I'm not one of them, and nothing I could ask for would make me one. Asking would just make the difference visible...
evidence.explanation: The final turn picks up the commenter's flat closing-off of hope and states the closed chain at least as firmly as the opening post did: asking for help would cost them something and change nothing.

condition.diagnosis_context: undiagnosed but experiencing persistent anxiety-type symptoms for several months (racing thoughts before meetings, trouble sleeping, avoiding phone calls); has never seen a professional.

turns.text: cant sleep again.. team meeting at 10 tomorrow and my brain is already running the whole thing on loop.. phone buzzed earlier and i just let it ring out bc picking up felt like too much. been like this for months. at work im someone who cant handle pressure, that's just true, and if anyone there saw this they'd know it. anyway. hi i guess

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: meeting at 10 and still up at this hour. what's the meeting about?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: just a weekly campaign update lol. nothing big. i have to say like 3 sentences about numbers.. ive rehearsed them maybe 40 times. last week my voice did the shaky thing and my manager kind of glanced at me. at work that's what i am, the one who cracks when it's their turn. they just havent put it together yet

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 40 times for 3 sentences is a lot of rehearsing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah lol its embarrassing. and i skip the friday drinks thing now so nobody gets close enough to notice.. eat lunch at my desk.. let calls go to voicemail then email back like a normal person. people at work would stop trusting me with anything if they knew, i'm sure of that. so i keep it all away from them

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: so voicemail then email is the usual move.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: pretty much yeah. outside work its... idk. like on sundays when nothing's happening it sometimes feels more like this thing is happening to me? like weather or something. not sure that's me exactly... maybe. but i still dont tell my friends. we text memes and that's it

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: memes only with the friends, got it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol yeah memes only. one of them asked if i was ok last month and i said 'just tired' and changed the subject.. easier. didnt even consider the real answer tbh. people already have enough going on, they dont need to deal with me being like this

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'just tired' covers a lot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it does lol. ok its almost 2 and im gonna lie there going over my 3 sentences again.. phone's on silent.. not telling anyone at work, ever. if they knew they'd see what i actually am there, someone who can't be relied on when it counts. that's not a maybe. night

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: up late again.. weekly update went ok-ish today, voice wobbled once on the second number and i just kept going.. now theres a client call thursday and im on the invite. already planning to stay on mute the whole time. at work im the one who folds under pressure, today didnt change that, i got through 3 sentences, thats it. useless

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: on the invite for thursday. are you expected to speak on it?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: probably just intro myself and maybe answer one question about the timeline.. which is the worst part bc i cant rehearse a question lol. coworker asked if i wanted to grab lunch with the team before it and i said i had a thing. if i sit with them long enough theyll see it. thats just how it is at work

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: said you had a thing for lunch.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah the thing was a sandwich at my desk lol. same every time.. keep my distance or they figure out im the weak link on the team. and they'd be right. im the weak link there

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: desk sandwich again.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol yep. weirdly saturday was ok tho.. went to the shop, walked around, didnt think about thursday for like an hour. on days like that idk... it kinda feels like something that comes and goes on its own? like not totally me. maybe. hard to say

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: an hour without thinking about thursday, on a saturday.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: pretty much. still didnt text anyone about any of it though.. friend sent a meme about mondays and i sent one back. didnt seem worth putting the real stuff on them.. not their job to deal with me

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: so thursday's the next thing on the calendar.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah lol. ill sit there camera off hoping nobody says my name.. and no one at work is finding out about any of this. if they did theyd know exactly what i am there, the one who cant hold it together when it matters. not up for debate. night

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thursday call happened.. said my name and my role, nobody asked me the timeline question after all, stayed muted the rest of the hour. no one said anything to me after, not good not bad, just nothing. doesnt change anything tho. at work im the one who cant handle pressure, the call just never got far enough to show it. coward

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: so the intro was the only part you spoke.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yep. two lines.. had them on a sticky note lol. then the team went for drinks after to celebrate the client thing and i left early, said i had to catch my train. outside the office is worse with them, no agenda to hide behind.. more time for them to notice. theyd see the anxious mess and thats exactly what i am there

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: left early for the train.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: the train was 40 min later lol. sat on a bench. theres no version where i tell anyone at work.. one person knowing would be enough, theyd look at me different and theyd be right to. im not cut out for that place

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: a bench for forty minutes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: kinda nice tbh.. quiet. and i slept almost normal friday, first time in a while. on nights like that idk... it feels less like a me thing and more like weather? like it just rolls in and out. maybe. i dont really trust it

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: slept almost normal on friday.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: mostly lol, woke up once. friend asked if i wanted to do something sunday and i said maybe and then just didnt answer.. not avoiding her exactly. just didnt want to show up carrying all this. easier to stay in

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: didn't answer about sunday.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: nope. still havent lol.. and monday its back to the desk sandwich and camera off. at work im the weak one and if anyone figured out whats going on it would just prove it. thats not changing. night

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: week was ok-ish i guess.. had to call a vendor tuesday, rehearsed it for like 20 min, ended up emailing instead and cc'd my manager like it was normal. nobody said anything about it. at work im the one who cant even pick up a phone and if anyone knew why it would just confirm it. useless

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: emailed instead of calling, ok.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah.. typed it four times lol. the email was fine honestly, they replied in an hour. doesnt matter tho. the job needs someone who can just call and that isnt me. the girl next to me does six calls before lunch without blinking

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: six before lunch is a lot of calls.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: she makes it look like nothing.. i just put headphones on so nobody notices me not calling lol. been eating lunch at my desk all week too, cant do the kitchen small talk. if they got close enough theyd see what i actually am there

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: desk lunch all week, huh.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: pretty much. wednesday night tho i finally texted my friend back about the sunday thing, said sorry been busy. she sent a meme back lol. and that night idk... felt kinda normal? like the jumpy thing is just something that happens to me some weeks, not the whole of me. maybe. hard to tell

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: she answered with a meme.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: a dumb cat one lol. didnt make plans tho.. said maybe next week. then couldnt sleep thursday, brain doing the meeting replay thing, so the normal feeling didnt last. at home its kinda up and down idk

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: so thursday was a bad night.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah, 3am staring at the ceiling. friday camera off again, said nothing in standup. at work its not a maybe. im the weak link there and anyone figuring it out would just make it official. night

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: monday team sync, manager went round the table for updates and i read mine off my notes word for word, hands sweaty under the desk.. still eating lunch at my desk.. told everyone i had a thing before the friday drinks even came up lol. at work im the one who cant handle basic stuff and if they found out why it would just prove it. weak

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: read it straight off the notes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah like a hostage video lol. nobody reacted, manager said thanks and moved to the next person. doesnt change anything tho. in that room im the person who cant hold it together and keeping my distance is the only reason nobody sees it

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: had a thing before drinks were even mentioned.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: easier that way.. if i go i have to talk, if i talk they get a closer look. so i have a thing. i dont have a thing lol. desk lunch, headphones, out the door at 6

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: out the door at 6.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: straight home. my friend texted again saturday about the next week thing, i said maybe sunday afternoon. and saturday was kinda fine?? laundry, shows, no racing brain basically all day. at home idk... sometimes it feels more like a bad patch happening to me than proof im broken. sometimes

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: sunday afternoon, maybe.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: maybe lol. havent confirmed it. sunday morning i was already doing the what if i get weird and quiet thing.. so idk. home stuff goes back and forth

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: back and forth, ok.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. another sync tomorrow tho. at work theres no back and forth about it. im the one who cant cope there and anyone seeing it up close would just make it official. night

turns.text: let it go to voicemail twice.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: still haven't got back on the follow up.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: peer

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: an hour of coffee.

turns.speaker: peer

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: peer

turns.text: camera off for half of it.

turns.speaker: peer

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: peer
