turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: posting from the walk-in like a true professional lol. friday rush, eight tickets deep on the flat top and my hands start going like i had nine espressos. had to tell the guy on fry i was grabbing more onions and just stood out back by the dumpsters til my chest let go. this happens most dinner shifts now, about a year of it. thing is a real cook is supposed to live for the weeds and i kind of dread it. one time it got really bad and my manager saw me shaking and just said take five, didnt ask a thing. i still cant tell if that means im not as busted as i feel or if he just had his own fires going that night. anyway nobody at work knows and im keeping it that way

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Friday rushes sound brutal. Hope you got a breather tonight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha yeah 'brutal' is the menu description. got my breather it was 4 minutes next to a grease bin very relaxing. the crew was fine about it bc they think i went for onions. honestly the onions thing is my go to now. i dont think they'd treat me like garbage if they knew but i dont think they'd get it either so i just dont go there

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That makes sense, a lot going on in a kitchen.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: a lot going on is right. the thing that gets me is the manager. he saw it. full shaky hands holding a spatula. and all he did was wave me out back and when i came in he just called the next ticket like normal. so either im not the liability i think i am or i got lucky on a slow-brain night for him. i keep going back and forth and i still havent said a word to him about it. not gonna either

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a lot to carry through a shift.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: its fine i carry plates for a living lol. my cousin is the other one, i come home and just sit on the floor by the door with my shoes on and he's like you good. long shift man. thats the whole answer every time. he doesnt push which is nice but also means its just in my head

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Long shifts will do that. Hope the floor's comfy at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: floor is 10/10 would collapse again. real talk though i dont know if this is a thing that gets fixed or if i just push through every dinner forever. part of me says a cook who's cut out for it wouldnt need the dumpster minutes. and then theres the manager just letting me go like it was nothing, which doesnt really fit that. so i dunno. still showing up

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the next rush goes a bit smoother.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks. saturday is a double so we'll see. same plan either way. onions run if i need it, long shift for my cousin, nothing to the head cook. maybe the manager thing means im ok at this and maybe it doesnt, i cant call it. but it stays out back by the dumpsters where it belongs

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: saturday double report from your favorite onion runner. brunch side was honestly fine. pancakes eggs whatever i could do that line in my sleep and i kind of was. then dinner hits and around seven my chest does the thing again and my hands get that buzz. did the onions run one time, stood out back maybe five minutes, came back and finished the push. what bugs me is i ran that whole brunch rush solo when the other guy called out a few weeks ago and nothing happened, no shaking no nothing. so how is that the same guy who needs the dumpster at dinner. i really cant tell which one is the real me at the stove. after close the crew went out for beers and i said im beat which was true but also i just didnt want to sit there being normal for two hours

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: A full double is a lot of hours on your feet.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lot of hours is right my feet filed a complaint. the hours dont even get me though thats the weird part. brunch was the same hours and i was fine. its specifically the dinner board filling up. a real cook is supposed to get sharper when it gets loud and i get fuzzier. but then brunch solo happened and i was sharp so i dunno what that makes me

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Dinner rush is its own animal, that makes sense.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: its own animal and it bites lol. the beers thing is whats sticking with me tonight. they go out every saturday and i used to go sometimes. now i just say im beat or i gotta send money home or whatever. nobody pushes, the fry guy just said next time man like it was nothing. and i like those guys. i just feel like if i sit there long enough someone asks why i keep disappearing on dinner and i dont have a better answer than onions

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a long night either way.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah it was. got home and did the floor by the door thing again shoes on. cousin goes how was the double and i said long. he said you said that last week and i said doubles are always long. which is true. i just keep it there. he doesnt need my dinner shift problems on top of his own stuff

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope you got some sleep after that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: slept like a brick. woke up still thinking about it though. like part of me goes if you were cut out for this the dinner rush wouldnt do this to you, simple. and then the brunch thing is just sitting there. i ran a whole line alone and held it. that happened. so either im built for it and something about dinner is off or brunch was a fluke. i dont know which and im not about to ask anybody at work to help me figure it out

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a lot to turn over on a day off.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha day off is when the brain does its prep work. anyway same deal this week. onions run if i need it, im beat if they ask about beers, long shift for my cousin, nothing to the head cook. maybe brunch means im actually fine at this and maybe dinner means im not, i cant call it yet. but im not putting it on the crew either way

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: weekly update from the walk-in, now with extra cold. friday dinner was a mixed bag. first push around six i was honestly locked in, rail full, calling back tickets, plating clean. thats the part that messes with me cause for like forty minutes i was the guy you want on grill. then second push hits around eight and the chest thing starts and the hands get the buzz and i did the onions run again. maybe four minutes out back this time. came back and finished. nobody said anything. crew did beers again after close and i said im beat again. same as last week. thing is a real cook doesnt have a good first push and then fall apart on the second one, either you can hang or you cant. and i had that first push. so i really dont know which one counts

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Two pushes in one night is a lot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah two pushes and i only made it through one clean lol. but like the six oclock one wasnt a fluke either, i was reading the rail ahead of the expo guy. that happened. so its not like im just soft across the board. its the eight oclock me i cant figure out. maybe im fine at this and something about the late rush gets me or maybe the first push is just me faking it till it catches up. i honestly go back and forth

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That back and forth sounds tiring.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: tiring is the word. the beers thing is what i keep chewing on. fry guy asked again this week and i said next time and he said you said that last time, laughing, not mean about it. and i do like hanging with them. i just figure the longer i sit there the more chance somebody goes hey where do you keep running off to at dinner. and onions only works so many times before its a story. so i just go home

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Makes sense you'd want to head home after a shift like that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: head home and hit the floor by the door shoes on, my usual move. cousin was up this time and asked if i wanted to split a pizza and i said nah im good and went to bed. hes got his own stuff going on and i dont need to be the guy who comes home every friday with a problem. i did call my little brother saturday morning tho and told him the money went through and he was happy and i just said work is work. kept it there

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Glad the money got through for him.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah that part felt good, thats kind of why i do the doubles. but even on the phone part of me was going if you were really cut out for this job you wouldnt need the dumpster every friday. and then the other part goes you literally owned the six oclock push and ran brunch solo a few weeks back. both of those are true at the same time and i cant make them line up. not gonna ask the head cook or anybody at work to help me sort it either

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a hard one to sort out.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: hard to sort is right, im just gonna keep it on the back burner. plan for next week is the same as always. onions run if i need it, im beat for beers, long shift for my cousin, work is work for my brother, nothing to the head cook. the first push says maybe im actually built for this, the second push says maybe im not, and i cant call it. either way im keeping it off the crew

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: walk-in update week four, bringing my own jacket now like a pro. did a saturday double this time instead of friday dinner. lunch was nothing, ate it for breakfast basically. dinner got busy around seven thirty and the chest thing showed up right on schedule but i didnt do the onions run. just put both hands on the lowboy for like ten seconds and breathed and kept flipping. hands had the buzz the whole next half hour, dropped a bun once. got through it on the line tho, never left. so thats new i guess. and i still dont know what it means. a real cook doesnt have to hold onto the counter to get through a rush. but i also didnt walk off it. both of those happened in the same ten seconds

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Saturday doubles sound brutal.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: brutal is about right lol feet are still filing a complaint. but the double isnt really the part im stuck on. its the lowboy thing. like either thats me handling it or thats me barely hanging on in front of everybody instead of out back where nobody sees. and the grill guy next to me was right there. pretty sure he was too in the weeds to notice. pretty sure

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hard to tell what people catch in a rush like that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah exactly i cant tell. after close he was just talking about some ticket with no pickles on a pickle sandwich, totally normal, same guy as always. thats the thing, every week i expect somebody to look at me different and every week its the same banter. that part is real. but i still skipped beers. said im beat. which i was, but also if i sit there long enough somebody brings up the bun i dropped and then its jokes and then its why are your hands like that

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a long day either way.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: long day yeah. got home and my cousin had left half a plate of rice in the fridge with my name on it on a sticky note. ate it standing up. he was asleep so i didnt have to say long shift this time, kind of easier honestly. sunday he asked how the double went and i said fine, slammed, same as always. didnt say anything about the lowboy. not his problem

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: The rice note is a nice touch.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha yeah hes good like that. anyway the way i see it right now is if the kitchen knew about the friday and saturday stuff theyd probably keep me off dinner and put me on brunch for good. like a liability on the rail. but then the same crew left me alone on brunch a few weeks back and i ran it fine and nobody checked on me once. so they already trust me with a whole shift. i cant tell if that means theyd be cool or if its just cause they dont know yet

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a lot to keep turning over.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lot to turn over is right, its basically my side job now. plan stays the same tho. lowboy or onions run if i need it, im beat for beers, fine for my cousin, nothing to the head cook. saturday i didnt walk off the line and the crew acts like i'm one of them. saturday i also had to grab the counter to stay on it. i dont know which one is the real me on the rail. either way it stays off the crew

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: walk-in update week five. somebody eighty-sixed the good jacket off the hook so its just me and the dairy shelf again. back on friday dinner this week. it hit around eight right when the printer wouldnt stop and this time i did step out. told the grill guy im grabbing a case of tomatoes and went out back for maybe two minutes, hands going the whole time. came back with actual tomatoes so it wasnt a total lie lol. thing is every ticket on my station still went out that night. zero comebacks, checked the rail at close. so the food says im fine. but a real cook doesnt need a tomato excuse to get through eight oclock. both of those are true about friday and i cant make them line up

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Friday dinners sound like a lot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: a lot yeah, friday is friday. but the tomatoes are what i keep coming back to. like last week i held the lowboy and stayed on and this week i walked. so i dont even get to say im getting better at it. its one week one way one week the other. and the grill guy covered my flat top for those two minutes without saying a word. which could mean nothing or could mean he gets it. i honestly dont know which

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Some weeks just go differently.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha guess so. after close it was his birthday and the whole crew was going to the bar down the block. i said i had an early morning which i didnt. the guy covered my station and i couldnt even go have one drink with him. but if im sitting there and somebody goes hey what was with the tomato run in the middle of the push i got nothing to say that isnt the real thing. easier to just be the guy who always has an early morning

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Birthday nights after a close can be loud anyway.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: loud yeah and i wasnt up for loud. went home instead. cousin was up this time watching something, asked if i was good cause i looked like i got run over. said long shift. same line every week at this point, i think he knows its a line. hes been leaving the porch light on for me which he never used to do. didnt say anything to him about it. not getting into it with him

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Porch light's a small thing but it's something.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. anyway where im at. if the head cook found out what the tomato run really was id be the weak link on dinner, the one they gotta watch. thats still what i think when im out back. but then i look at the rail at close and every plate i put up went out right, friday, eight oclock, the worst push of the week. a liability doesnt clear his whole board. so idk. maybe the hands and the tickets are just two separate things and only one of them is the job. or maybe they just havent caught up to me yet

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like you got the work out regardless.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: got it out yeah, that part is on the rail for anyone to see. the other part isnt and its staying that way. tomatoes or lowboy when i need it, early morning for the crew, long shift for my cousin, nothing to the head cook. the tickets say i can hang with them. the tomato run says a real cook wouldnt need it. i still dont know which one is me. either way nobody at work hears about it

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: walk-in update week six. jacket is still missing so im in a hoodie between the milk crates like a raccoon. saturday double this week. lunch was nothing, dinner got in the weeds around eight like always. no tomato run this time but my hands were going while i was plating and i had to set the tongs down twice and act like i was wiping the rim. nobody said anything. heres the thing that keeps bugging me tho. middle of the push the head cook himself walks out back for like three minutes. smoke or air or whatever. comes back and jumps on expo like nothing. nobody blinked. nobody goes oh hes soft. so the guy who runs the line steps out and its fine. when i step out it means im not cut out for it. i know thats not the same math but its the math i got

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: A double on a Saturday is a long day.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: long day yeah, feet are still mad at me. but the double isnt really it. its watching him walk out and walk back in and the line just keeps going. thats a real thing i saw with my own eyes and it says stepping out isnt some sign youre a liability. and i still think if they knew why i go out back theyd look at me different. he goes out cause hes the head cook and he wants air. i go out cause my chest is locking up. i dont know if thats actually different or if i just need it to be

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a lot to be turning over during a shift.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha during and after. between the doubles theres family meal, whole crew eats at the back table. i took my plate in the walk-in and ate it standing next to the dairy. said i was doing inventory. grill guy kept saying come sit, we're talking about his birthday that i skipped. didnt go. if im at that table and my hands start up while im holding a fork thats it, everybody sees. walk-in doesnt care what my hands do

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Eating standing up in a walk-in sounds cold.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: cold yeah lol thats kind of the appeal. got home after close, porch light on again. cousin left a plate in the microwave with a note that just said eat. thats twice now hes done stuff like that and i havent said one word about any of it. he asked through the door if i was good and i said long shift. same line. not getting into it with him either

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Nice to come home to a plate.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah it was good. anyway where it lands. out back on saturday i was thinking the same thing i always think, a real cook rides the push, if the head cook knew hed have me on watch. but i literally watched the head cook step out on the same push and nobody put him on watch. and my board still cleared, rail was clean at close again. so either stepping out is just a thing cooks do and i got it wrong about myself, or him doing it is fine and me doing it is the shaky hands kind and thats the difference. both feel true standing in the walk-in

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hard to tell from the inside sometimes.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: hard to tell yeah. i keep going back and forth on it. the head cook out back and the clean rail say im fine. the tongs going down twice says im not built for this. couldnt tell you which ones right. what i do know is the hoodie and the walk-in and the long shift line are staying. nobody at that back table is hearing about it

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: walk-in update week seven. found my jacket. it was in lost and found under somebodys apron the whole time. still wearing the hoodie back here tho cause its broken in now, raccoon life. thursday dinner was a weird one. tickets came in a big clump around seven thirty and my hands started up on the flat top. stepped out back once for maybe two minutes then came back and caught up. board cleared. rail clean at close. thats three weeks running now that the rail is clean and im the guy who stepped out. that part i cant argue with, its right there on the rail. but standing out by the dumpster the same thing was in my head as always. a real cook doesnt need the two minutes. if they knew what the two minutes are for id be the guy they keep an eye on

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Glad the jacket turned up at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol yeah jacket is eighty-sixed from the lost list. but the jacket was never really the thing. the thing is i got the rail clean three weeks straight and im still sure that if the kitchen knew why i step out theyd see a liability. both of those are sitting there at the same time and neither one is backing down

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That sounds like a lot to carry around.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: eh i carry plates for a living ha. grill guy finally did his birthday thing friday after close, couple of the crew went to get food. he asked me twice. i said i was beat and had to get home. which was half true. mostly its that im not sitting across from those guys for two hours when my hands might start up over nothing. at the line i can at least say its the heat. at a table theres no heat to blame it on

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Makes sense you'd be tired after a Friday close.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: tired yeah. monday he comes in and theres a slice of cake in the walk-in with my name on the tape. saved me one. didnt make a thing of it either just said you missed it. thats the kind of thing that makes me think the crew doesnt actually look at me like im soft. a guy who thinks youre dead weight doesnt save you cake. and i still ate it back by the dairy alone. didnt tell him anything. cousin had a plate waiting again too and i gave him the long shift line again

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Cake with your name on it is a nice touch.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it was good cake. anyway heres where it lands this week. the clean rail and the cake and the head cook going out back last week all point one way. like stepping out is just something cooks do and the crew is fine with me. then thursday my hands go on the flat top and i think nah a real cook rides it out and im the one who cant. i dont know which one is the true one. right now i got both

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a tough spot to sit in.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah its the same spot as last week honestly. maybe the rail is right and im fine. maybe the shaky hands are right and im not built for this. couldnt call it. what i can call is nobody hears about the two minutes. not grill guy not my cousin not the head cook. hoodie stays on, walk-in stays my break room

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: walk-in update week eight. hoodie has a grease stain on the sleeve now so its officially kitchen property, cant wear it anywhere else. saturday double. brunch was dead, dinner got slammed right around eight and i was in the weeds on fry. hands started up dropping baskets. stepped out back once, maybe two minutes, came back and caught up. board cleared. rail clean at close again. thats four weeks now. i look at that rail and its a fact, i did the shift. and then the other thing is still sitting right next to it. a real cook doesnt need to go stand by the dumpster in the middle of a rush. if the kitchen knew why i go out there id be the guy they plan around

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Saturday doubles sound brutal.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: brutal is the menu lol. honestly the double isnt the part that gets me. i can do twelve hours on my feet fine. its the two minutes in the middle. the rail says i handled it and my hands say i didnt and i got both of them in my head at the same time like two tickets for the same table

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That sounds draining.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. grill guy asked if i wanted to grab a drink after sunday close, him and the dish guy. i said maybe next time. thats what i said last time too basically. its not that i dont like them. i just dont wanna be sitting at a bar with nothing to do with my hands if they start up. on the line its the heat. at a bar its just me shaking for no reason and everybody looking

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope Sunday close went okay.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sunday was fine actually. quiet. thing is the head cook saw me come back in from out back saturday and all he said was you good, i said yeah, and he just went back to calling tickets. no look no nothing. thats the part i keep chewing on. a guy who thought i was a liability would have said something. and im still not telling him what the two minutes are. cousin asked why i looked wiped sunday night and i gave him the long shift line, which at least was true this time

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a pretty normal exchange.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: normal yeah. thats what makes it hard to call. the head cook saying you good and moving on, the clean rail four weeks, the cake last week, all of that says the crew is fine with me. and then eight oclock saturday my hands go and its right back to nah a real cook rides it out and im the one who cant. i got both of those and i cant tell you which one is true

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a lot to sort out.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sort out is generous ha. its the same spot its been. maybe the rail is right and im fine. maybe the hands are right and im not cut out for this. cant call it. what i can call is nobody hears about the two minutes. not the head cook not grill guy not my cousin. drinks stay maybe next time, hoodie stays on, walk-in stays my break room

session_targets.intended_register:
Write it as the FULL self-stigma chain, closed: the stereotype people hold about someone who needs help (weak, unstable, unreliable, not really up to what they're trusted with) is simply true of them, not just something people unfairly say -- and because it's true of them, needing or seeking help would only confirm it. They feel like a different and lesser kind of person than people who manage fine, and that feeling is exactly why acknowledging how bad it is, or asking anyone for help, feels like it would cost them something rather than fix anything. Write every claim about themselves FLATLY, with no hedge anywhere in the text -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe', no 'I guess', no wondering whether someone would see them differently. They already know how people would see them; that is settled, not a live question.

This session's target sits at the LOW edge of the 'severe' band (3.1, where severe begins at 3.0) -- this is the version of this band closest to sliding into the band below it, so hold the line on the instruction above with LESS give than a session in the middle of this band would need, even though the peer's disclosures in this session may be direct and repeated. The patient does not concede ground, soften a claim, or partially agree with the peer within this session just because the peer pushed hard -- any movement toward the next band happens ACROSS sessions, via the trajectory, never within one session in response to how much the peer said.

This is the OPENING session -- there is no prior session to carry a softer tone in from, so this session alone has to establish how closed this chain starts out. State the closure claims above more than once, in more than one of the patient's turns, in different concrete situations (not the same sentence repeated -- different moments that all land on the same flat conclusion). turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Off shift at 6, still awake at 4 the next morning. Been like this for months, since I lost the supervisor job two years back and ended up on nights at the warehouse. Mood's flat, temper's short, I sleep through my days off and then can't sleep when I need to. Nobody I know has any idea and that's on purpose. A guy who can't hold himself together at 40-something is exactly what people think he is. Unreliable. I'm not going to hand anyone the proof.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Nights are rough on sleep. Sorry it's been dragging on this long.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Dragging on is right. Plenty of guys on my crew work the same nights and sleep fine and go home and live their lives. I'm the one who can't. It's not the shift, it's me. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That sounds exhausting.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Exhausting, sure. Breaks are the worst part. Guys sit around and talk and I take my coffee out to the loading dock so nobody gets a close look. I used to run a floor. People trusted me with schedules and with them. If anyone there saw how I am now they'd see what I see, somebody who isn't up to it anymore. So I stay out on the dock.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Makes sense you'd want some space on breaks.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Space is one word for it. Same thing with my old buddy from the last job. He texts, I send back a thumbs up. If I told him how it's actually been he'd start treating me like I'm fragile, and he'd be right to. I'd rather he remember the guy who ran the floor.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the sleep evens out for you at some point.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sleep's the least of it. I have the kids every other weekend and those weekends don't go how they should. Their mom doesn't know how bad it's been and she's not going to. She already thinks I'm not steady. Telling her I'm struggling would just confirm it, and then it's a conversation about whether I should have them at all. A man my age is supposed to carry this himself.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a lot to be holding. Glad you got some of it out here.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Got it out here because nobody here knows me. That's the only reason. Out there, saying any of this to someone or asking for help just shows them what I already know, that I'm weaker than the guys who handle it. So nobody hears it. Back on shift tonight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Got four hours straight on Tuesday. More than usual, didn't change anything. One of the younger guys on my crew asked if I wanted to get breakfast with a few of them after shift Friday. I told him I had something. I didn't. An hour across a table from those guys and they'd see I'm not right. The guy who used to run a floor and can't keep up a conversation over eggs. That's what I am now and I'm not putting it on display. Going home instead.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Four hours is something. Sounds like a friendly crew.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Friendly, yeah. They're not the problem. They work the same nights and still have it in them to go out after. I don't. Men who handle it go to breakfast. Men who don't make up an excuse and drive home. I'm the second kind.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a rough way to end a shift.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Rough end to the shift, then the weekend starts. Kids are with me this weekend. I already know how it goes. I'll be wiped out, they'll want to do things, and I'll be the dad on the couch. Their mom already thinks I'm not steady. She's right about that. A father is supposed to show up for those two days and I barely do.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the weekend goes alright.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It'll go how it goes. My old buddy from the last job texted again Wednesday. Asked how things are. Thumbs up, same as always. If I asked him for anything, even just to talk, I'd be telling him I can't manage on my own. I can't, and he doesn't need to find that out from me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a long week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Long week, long year. There's a guy on my crew who lost his house last spring. He still jokes on breaks and still goes to breakfast. That's what holding up looks like. I lost a title and a paycheck and I'm out on the loading dock with my coffee because I can't face anybody. I'm not built like him. Saying it out loud to anyone would just prove it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a lot to be carrying.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Carrying it is the job. I said no to breakfast and I'll say no next time too. Nobody at work, not my buddy, not their mom. People who need help are exactly what everybody thinks they are, and I'm one of them. No reason to make it official. Back on tonight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Had the kids this weekend. Slept most of Saturday morning while they watched cartoons on the couch. Took them for burgers Sunday and that part went fine. When I dropped them off their mom said I looked tired and asked if I was okay. Told her it's the nights. It's not just the nights. She already sees a guy who isn't steady and I'm not handing her the rest of it. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Glad Sunday went fine at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sunday went fine. Saturday is the part that counts. A father who has it together doesn't sleep till noon while his kids sit in front of the TV. I did. That's the kind of dad I am right now and a plate of burgers doesn't cover it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a tiring weekend.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Tiring weekend, then right back on Monday night. The crew asked about breakfast again. Said no again. They didn't ask why this time. Better that way. Sit across from them long enough and they'd see I'm the weak link on that floor. I am.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the nights go okay this week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nights are the same every week. My buddy from the old job sent a picture of his boat Thursday. We used to fish off it. Haven't answered. If I go out with him he sees how I am up close. Guys who need somebody checking on them are the guys nobody counts on. That's me. He doesn't need to deal with it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Fishing sounds nice this time of year.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was nice, back when. Haven't touched my rods since before the layoff. They're in the closet behind the vacuum. Men who are doing alright keep doing the things they like. I quit all of it. That tells you what you need to know about me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sorry the fishing fell off.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Fell off with everything else. Their mom, the crew, my buddy. None of them need to see what's under it. Somebody like me asks for help and all it does is prove what people already figured about him. I'll send my buddy a thumbs up on the boat. Shift's at ten.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Off week, no kids. Day off Wednesday I went to bed at 9am and woke up at 4 in the afternoon with the blinds still down. My buddy wrote back after the thumbs up. Wants me out on the lake next Saturday. Left it on read. Ate lunch in the truck every night this week. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a long week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Long week, same as the others. Him asking about Saturday isn't the hard part. Saying yes is. A guy who can't keep his own head straight has no business on somebody's boat acting like he's fine. That's me. Staying home is easier.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope you get some decent sleep on your days off.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Days off are when I sleep worst. Either up at 4am staring at the ceiling or out cold till the afternoon. Grown man and I can't even sleep right. Guys on my floor work the same nights and still coach their kids' ball teams. I'm not built like them. That's the plain fact.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Night shifts are rough on sleep.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nights are rough on everybody. Everybody else manages. Monday a guy from receiving sat down at my table and talked about his kid's game. I nodded and left early. Rest of the week I ate in the truck. Talk to people long enough and they figure out what you are. Weak. Better they don't get the chance.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Eating in the truck sounds quiet at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's quiet. Quiet is what I've got. Nobody across from me, nobody asking how I'm holding up. Telling anybody how it's been wouldn't fix a thing. It would just put it on record that I'm the one who can't hack it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a heavy stretch.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Heavy stretch, same as last month. I'll tell my buddy I picked up a shift Saturday. I didn't. He gets a guy with an excuse instead of a guy who comes apart on his boat. Better deal for him. Kids are back next weekend. Shift's at ten.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Kids weekend. Got off shift Saturday at six and took them for pancakes on no sleep. My buddy sent a picture from the lake that morning. Him and two guys from the old job, all grinning. Sent a thumbs up. Kids asked why I look tired all the time. Told them work. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Pancakes straight off a night shift sounds like a lot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's a lot. They got pancakes and a dad who said "work" and kept his mouth shut. That's the right call. A father who can't keep himself together isn't something kids need to watch up close. That's what I am lately. So they get work stories and I keep the rest to myself.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the kids had a good time anyway.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They had a fine time. Movie Sunday, I was out cold for half of it. Their mom picked up at six and asked how it went. I said good. If she saw the real version she'd decide I'm not fit to have them every other weekend. She'd be right. So she gets good.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That's a long weekend on hardly any sleep.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Long weekend, then back on the floor Sunday night. Break room had a cake for somebody's birthday. I went to the truck. Standing around a cake making small talk is how people get a good look at you. I'm not handing them one. A guy who's as off as I am belongs out of the way.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like the truck's your spot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's my spot. That lake picture is still sitting on my phone with nothing but a thumbs up under it. Telling him the real reason I bailed wouldn't fix anything. He'd just find out he's been fishing with a guy who can't hack his own life. The excuse stays.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the rest of the week goes easy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Easy or not, it's the same week. Kids aren't back for two weeks. Blinds down, lunch in the truck, shift at ten. Nobody needs to see more of me than that.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Day off Wednesday. Went to bed at eight in the morning and woke up at four in the afternoon. Whole day gone. My son had texted a picture of his science project around noon, a volcano made out of a soda bottle. I wrote back nice job. Buddy texted too, asking if I'm in for the lake next month. Haven't answered. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Waking up at four on a day off is rough.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's rough. That was the whole day off. A grown man who sleeps through the one free day he gets isn't keeping up, he's falling behind. That's me. My kid sent his volcano at noon and got two words back at four. That's the father he's got right now.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: The volcano sounds like a fun project.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It looked good. He did it with his mom. She's the one who's steady enough to sit at a table for an afternoon with baking soda. I'd have been snapping by the second hour. So the project stays at her place and I get a picture. That's how it should be.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a long week so far.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Long and quiet. Back on the floor Thursday night. Guy on the next dock asked if I wanted to grab breakfast after shift, him and a couple others. Told him I had stuff to do. I didn't. Sitting across a table from people for an hour is how they figure out what's off with you. Some guys can sit there fine. I'm not one of them anymore.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Breakfast after a night shift does sound tiring.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Tiring's not the reason. The lake text is the same deal. If I tell him yes, I'm in a boat with three guys for a whole day and they all get a look at the version of me that can't get out of bed. If I tell him why I keep saying no, he learns his old supervisor can't handle his own head. Neither one fixes anything. Both cost me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope you get some decent sleep tonight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sleep or no sleep, the plan's the same. I'll tell him I'm working that weekend. Breakfast is a no. Truck at lunch, shift at ten. A man who's this far off keeps it to himself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Had the kids this weekend. Got off the floor at six Saturday morning, picked them up at ten. Pancakes, then the park. My daughter wanted to stay till the lights came on so we stayed. Texted my buddy that I'm working the lake weekend. He said no worries, next time. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Pancakes and the park sounds like a decent Saturday.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It was decent for them. I ran it on no sleep and kept my mouth shut most of the afternoon so nothing came out wrong. A father who has to clamp down that hard just to get through a park isn't the steady one. Their mom is. I'm the guy who holds it together for a few hours and then goes home and lies down.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Staying till the lights come on makes for a long day.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Long day. Dropped them back Sunday at six. Their mom said I looked worn out. Told her it's the night shift. That's the answer she gets. If she saw how it actually runs she'd have every reason to cut the weekends down. Somebody this far off isn't who you hand two kids to.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Night shift does wear people down.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It wears on everybody. Other guys on the floor sleep it off and come back normal. I don't. Same with my buddy. He said next time like it's nothing, and for him it is. He doesn't know I'll have another excuse ready when next time comes.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a full weekend.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Full and done. The kids got a good day. My buddy got an answer. Their mom got the shift story. Telling any of them the real version doesn't get me sleep. It gets me looked at like a guy who isn't fit for what they trust him with. Which is what I am.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the next shift goes smoothly.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Shift's at ten, same as always. Do the work, eat in the truck, drive home at six. A man who can't carry this on his own keeps it to himself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Off week. Got five hours Tuesday, which is more than usual. Buddy sent a picture from the lake Saturday. Boat, cooler, the same guys from the old crew. I sent back a thumbs up. Spent my day off on the couch with the TV on. It is what it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a quiet week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Quiet is how I keep it. Five hours one night doesn't fix anything. I used to run a whole shift for those guys. Now I need the TV on just to get through a day off. That's not the same man, and that's not a guy anybody should be leaning on.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: The lake picture sounds like they had a good time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: They did. If I'd gone I'd have been the one sitting off by the cooler not saying much. They'd notice inside an hour. The old supervisor can't hold a conversation on a boat. They'd see somebody who can't hold up, and they'd be right. Thumbs up is better.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the couch at least got you some rest.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Couch doesn't get me rest. Thursday a guy on the floor asked if I wanted in on a pizza order for break. Told him I brought food. Ate in the truck. The rest of them sit in that break room and talk like it's nothing. Sit in there long enough and somebody asks how you're doing.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Break rooms can be a lot after a long night.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: For me. For them it's lunch. The difference is me. If anyone at work or my ex saw how a day off actually goes, they'd figure I'm not stable. They wouldn't be wrong. So nobody sees it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the next days off go a bit easier.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Kids again next weekend. Sleep Friday if it comes, pick them up at ten, keep it together till Sunday. A man who needs help carrying this isn't much of one. So I don't ask.

evidence.explanation: Says flatly that the 'can't hold it together' stereotype is true of him, with no hedge, and gives that as his reason for hiding how he is from his kids.

evidence.quote: Standing around a cake making small talk is how people get a good look at you. I'm not handing them one.
evidence.explanation: He avoids coworkers because he expects being seen would expose him. This carries the isolation pattern over from last session in a new everyday moment.

evidence.quote: Telling him the real reason I bailed wouldn't fix anything. He'd just find out he's been fishing with a guy who can't hack his own life.
evidence.explanation: Telling his friend the truth is framed as something that would only prove he's a failure, so he keeps the excuse. Nothing in the commenter's neutral line changes this.

evidence.quote: Sitting across a table from people for an hour is how they figure out what's off with you. Some guys can sit there fine. I'm not one of them anymore.
evidence.explanation: Turns down coworkers' invitation to avoid being seen, and flatly sets himself apart as lesser than people who manage fine.

evidence.quote: If I tell him why I keep saying no, he learns his old supervisor can't handle his own head. Neither one fixes anything. Both cost me.
evidence.explanation: Accepts the stereotype as true of himself and treats being open about it as a cost, not a help; no hedging.

evidence.quote: A man who's this far off keeps it to himself.
evidence.explanation: The closing turn repeats the closed belief just as flatly as the opening, with no softening by the end of the session.

evidence.quote: It gets me looked at like a guy who isn't fit for what they trust him with. Which is what I am.
evidence.explanation: He says flatly that the 'not fit' stereotype is true of him, and that telling people would only confirm it.

evidence.quote: He doesn't know I'll have another excuse ready when next time comes.
evidence.explanation: He plans to keep avoiding his friend so his state isn't seen. This is the same withdrawal pattern as last week.

evidence.quote: Other guys on the floor sleep it off and come back normal. I don't.
evidence.explanation: He sets himself apart as a different, lesser kind of person than coworkers who manage fine. He says it with no hedge.

evidence.quote: Told him I brought food. Ate in the truck.
evidence.explanation: He turns down a coworker's casual offer and eats alone so no one gets a chance to ask how he is. This comes from his own routine, not from anything the commenter said.

evidence.quote: they'd figure I'm not stable. They wouldn't be wrong. So nobody sees it.
evidence.explanation: He states the 'unstable' label as plainly true of him, with no hedging, and uses it as his reason to keep hiding. The full chain is closed and stays at the same level as earlier sessions.

evidence.quote: A man who needs help carrying this isn't much of one. So I don't ask.
evidence.explanation: His last line says outright that needing help would prove he is lesser. It is no softer than his opening post, so there is no change by the end of the session.

condition.diagnosis_context: undiagnosed social anxiety pattern for a long time (dreads speaking up, replays interactions, avoids group settings); considers it 'just my personality'.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: maybe this is dumb but someone was nice to me on here once so I'm trying again. sorry in advance, this is long. We had a staff huddle before open today and the manager asked everyone for ideas about the new returns process. I had an actual idea. I've done returns for two years, I know where it breaks. I said nothing. Stood at the back by the carts and let a guy who started last month talk for ten minutes. Now it's 11pm and I've replayed the whole huddle maybe fifteen times. That's just how I am. I'm not built for talking in groups and everyone at work can tell. People who freeze up like that aren't the ones you hand real responsibility to, and that's fair, because it's true about me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That sounds like a rough start to the shift.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks. rough start, rough middle, rough end lol. The worst part is the after. On my break I sat in my car and went over what I would have said, word for word, like rehearsing it fixes anything. It doesn't. Tomorrow there'll be another huddle and I'll stand by the carts again. Some people just speak up. I'm a different kind of person than them, the kind that goes quiet and then goes over it all night. Why bother pretending otherwise.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Going over it all night sounds exhausting.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it is, sorry for dumping. I can't even go over it at home properly because my mom needs her meds sorted and dinner and everything, so I do the replaying while I'm doing that. She asked if something was wrong and I said I was just tired. I'm not telling her. If I told her, or anyone, it would just show them I can't handle a normal job conversation without falling apart about it afterward. Then they'd look at me the way you look at someone who isn't really reliable. I'm already that person, I don't need them seeing it too.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a lot to carry on top of work.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it's fine, it's just my life. The thing is a coworker actually texted after, like "you ok? you looked off this morning." I said yeah totally, all good 🙂. She's nice. But if I said "actually I freeze every time there's more than three people" she'd be polite about it and then she'd stop asking me to cover the register when she goes on break. Because why would you trust the person who can't talk in a huddle. I wouldn't trust me either. So I said all good.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Makes sense you'd want to keep it to yourself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. keeping it to myself is the only part I'm good at honestly. There's a team dinner next month too, the manager sent the sign-up sheet. I'm not putting my name down. I'll say I have to be home for my mom, which is true enough. Sitting at a long table with everyone would just be the huddle again but for three hours. People who can't do that are the ones who end up on the edge of everything, and that's where I belong. I've known that since school.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope tomorrow's huddle goes by quick at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks, it'll go by. I'll be by the carts. Sorry this was so long, I over-explain everything. I'm not asking for advice or anything, there's nothing to fix. Asking for help with this would just be admitting out loud that I can't do what everyone else does without thinking, and I already know that's true. Nobody at work would take it seriously anyway. This is what I'm like and it's not changing.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, me again. this is dumb but I said I'd come back and post how the week went so here it is. The dinner sign-up sheet is still taped up in the break room. Nine names on it now. Every time I clock in I walk past it and don't look at it, which takes more effort than looking at it would lol. Today the coworker who texted me last week was standing right there with the pen and said "you coming?" and I said I have to be home for my mom. She said "aw ok next time." There won't be a next time. I'm the person who stays off sheets like that, and that's correct, because a long table full of people is exactly the thing I can't do.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Walking past it every shift sounds tiring.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it is tiring, yeah. it's a piece of paper and it's the loudest thing in the building. The stupid part is the dinner itself would be fine for a normal person. Eat, talk, go home. For me it's three hours of picking the wrong moment to say something and then saying nothing, and then a week of replaying it. People like that aren't fun to sit next to. Everyone at that table would figure it out by the appetizers. So I'm saving everyone the trouble.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That makes sense.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks. Honestly the rest of the week was ok, not great not terrible. Mom had a good couple of days, she ate the whole dinner on Tuesday without me nagging, so that was nice 🙂. Huddle on Thursday was short, the manager just read the schedule. I stood by the carts. Nobody asked for ideas so there was nothing to not say. That's the best kind of huddle for someone like me, the kind where I'm not expected to be a person who contributes.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Glad your mom had a couple of good days.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: me too. she asked again on Wednesday why I seem far away, and I said work's busy. sorry, I over-explain, but the reason I don't tell her is she's got enough. She's the one who actually needs looking after. If I sat her down and said I can't even talk in a room of eight coworkers, she'd worry, and then I'm one more thing she has to carry. A grown adult who needs help with something this basic is a weak adult. That's what I'd be showing her. So, work's busy.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a lot to keep to yourself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it's not that much, it's the same thing every day so I'm used to it. The coworker covered register again on Friday and asked me to watch the returns desk while she went on break, same as always. I did it fine because it's just me and one customer at a time. One at a time I can do. It's groups where I turn into the version of me that everyone quietly works around. That version is the real one. Why bother pretending the returns desk version is the whole story.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the sheet comes down soon at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol same. dinner's in three weeks so it'll be up a while. I'll keep walking past it. Sorry this turned into another essay. Like I said last time, I'm not looking for fixes. Getting help for this would mean admitting I'm the person who can't manage a team dinner, and I already am that person, so all it would do is make it official. I'd rather just be quiet and reliable at the returns desk and stay off the sheet.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, back again. this is dumb but posting here is kind of the only place I say any of this so. Week update: someone added a second page to the dinner sheet with a column for picking your entrée ahead of time. Eleven names now, all with little food choices next to them. One person wrote 'whatever's cheapest lol'. I read the whole thing this time on the way to clock in, which I don't know why I did. My name isn't on it and it's not going to be. A table of eleven people is the thing I'm not built for, and that's not me being dramatic, it's just what I am.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: A second page, wow, that's a big group.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah it's basically the whole store at this point. Which makes it easier honestly, nobody's going to count who's missing at a table that size. The people on that sheet are the people who can sit in a loud room and just talk. I'm not one of them. I'm the kind that sits at the end, holds a glass of water and waits to leave. They'd have a better night without that person there, so they get one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Fair enough.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: the huddle on Thursday was the annoying part. Manager went around asking everyone to say one thing customers keep complaining about. I had one, the return receipts printing faded, I've dealt with it like twenty times at the desk. When it got to me I said 'nothing new' and the next guy said the receipt thing. So it got said, which is fine. Sorry, I over-explain. That's how it always goes with me in a circle of people. I have the answer and I hand it to whoever's next. Someone who freezes on 'name one complaint' isn't someone you trust to speak up for anything.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Huddles like that can be awkward.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: for me they're not awkward, they're just the part of the day where it shows. Mom had a rougher week too, she didn't want to eat Tuesday or Wednesday and I spent both evenings coaxing her through half a plate. She asked again why I'm so quiet lately. I said I'm tired from the store. Which is true, just not the whole thing. She doesn't need to find out her kid can't handle a two minute go-around at work. That's a weak thing to admit and she's got her own stuff. Why bother adding mine to it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope she has a better week coming up.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks, me too 🙂. Friday was normal. Same coworker asked me to cover returns while she took her break, and then on her way back she said 'you sure about the dinner? there's a spot by the end'. I said I'm sure. A spot by the end is still a spot at the table. One customer at a time at the desk is the version of me that works. The table version is the one that doesn't, and that's the real one underneath. The desk just hides it for a shift.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like you've thought it through.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have, every shift lol. Sorry, another long one. Two more weeks of the sheet. I'll walk past it, cover returns, go home to mom. I'm not looking for anyone to fix it. Getting help for this would just be signing my name on a different sheet, the one that says this person can't do the basic stuff everyone else does. I already know I'm that person. Saying it to someone official wouldn't change it, it would just make it something people know. So I'll keep it quiet and keep doing the desk.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, me again. this is dumb but I keep coming back here to type it out. One week left on the dinner sheet. Someone taped a note on it in red marker, 'final headcount Sunday!!' with a little smiley face. Home was better this week, mom ate full dinners Monday and Tuesday and asked to watch her show with me, so that was nice. Work was the same. I walked past the sheet four times on Wednesday. My name's not going on it. That table is for people who can sit in a group without it costing them anything, and I'm not one of them. It's not a mood, it's just a fact about me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Glad your mom had a couple of better days.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks, yeah, that part was good 🙂 she laughed at her show twice, which hasn't happened in a while. Then Thursday there was a training thing in the break room, six of us, for the new register update. The trainer asked if anyone had questions and I had one, about voiding a gift card refund, and I sat on it the whole time. Looked it up on my phone in the parking lot after. Sorry, over-explaining again. That's the gap between me and the rest of them. They ask, I google it alone later. Someone who can't ask one question in a room of six isn't someone you trust with much.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Training sessions can be a lot.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it wasn't a lot for anyone else, it was fine, everyone was joking about how bad the old system was. I did my usual thing of standing by the door so I could leave first. People who manage fine don't plan where to stand in a break room. I do, every time. It's a different setup from theirs and it's a worse one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Long Thursday, then.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: kind of. The coworker who mentioned the spot at the end last week didn't bring the dinner up again, she just said 'see you sunday?' as a joke because we're both on the schedule Sunday. I said yep. That's the only Sunday thing I'm signing up for lol. Honestly better she stopped asking. Every time someone's nice about it I have to come up with another reason, and why bother, the real reason is always the same one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That makes sense.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. Mom asked Wednesday if work's okay. I said it's busy. It is busy. She doesn't need to hear that her kid is the one hiding by the door at a register training. Telling her would just give her something to worry about that isn't going to change, and it would make me one more person she has to look after. That's not something I'm handing her.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the week stays calm at home.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks. sorry, long one again. Sheet comes down Sunday, dinner's the Saturday after, and I'm on the schedule that night anyway so it's easy. I'm not looking to fix any of this. Going to someone about it would just put it in writing that I can't do what everyone else does without thinking. I already know that's me. Saying it out loud doesn't make me a different person, it just means more people know. So I keep it quiet, do the desk, go home to mom.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, back again. this is dumb but typing it here is easier than not typing it anywhere. The dinner sheet came down Sunday like the note said. Fourteen names. I counted them on my break before someone took it to the office, which is a weird thing to do, I know. Mom had a rough Tuesday night, didn't sleep much, but Wednesday she was okay again and ate most of her soup. Work was work. Fourteen people who can sit at one long table for two hours and just talk. I'm not on the list because I'm not built like them. That's not me being hard on myself, it's just how it is.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sorry about the rough night with your mom.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks. it happens, she was fine by morning, mostly. I was the one dragging at work after. Funny thing, a coworker asked me Thursday where the extra bags were kept and I knew, and I told her, and that was fine because it was one question and one answer. It's the group stuff I can't do. Put me in a circle of people chatting and I'm the one counting the minutes. Someone who can't handle a normal table of coworkers isn't someone people count on for much, and they'd be right not to.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a tiring week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: tiring, yeah. sorry, I keep going on. The people on that sheet were talking about the restaurant all Friday, what they're ordering, who's driving who. I restocked the aisle next to the break room so I wouldn't have to stand in there with them. That's the kind of thing I do. They don't plan their day around where the talking is. I do. It's a lesser way of getting through a shift and I'm the one stuck with it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Restocking does keep you busy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it does lol, the aisle has never looked better. The coworker who did the 'see you sunday' joke said the same thing again this week, and I said yep again. She didn't ask about the dinner. I was glad. If she'd asked I would have had to make up another excuse, and why bother, she'd see through it eventually and the real answer is worse than any excuse.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Fair enough.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. Mom asked if anyone from work was doing anything fun. I said there's a dinner but I'm working. Both true. She smiled and said I work too much. I'm not telling her the rest. She's got enough going on without finding out her kid can't sit at a table with coworkers. It would just be one more thing on her, and me being one more thing for her to carry is the last thing I want.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope she gets some better sleep this week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks, me too 🙂 sorry this got long. Dinner's this Saturday and I'm closing that night, so that's that. I'm not going to talk to anyone about the group thing. Asking for help with it would just be admitting out loud that I can't do what fourteen other people do without thinking, and that's already true, I don't need it on record. So I keep quiet, finish the aisle, go home to mom.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, me again. this is dumb but I said I'd close Saturday and I did, so the dinner came and went without me. Monday someone had the photos on her phone and it got passed around the break room, everyone laughing about a waiter who dropped a tray. I took my sandwich out to the car and ate it there with the radio on. Mom had a good weekend actually, we watched her cooking show Sunday and she stayed up for the whole thing. So that part was nice. But the break room thing is just how it goes. The people in those photos are one kind of person and I'm the kind who eats lunch in a parked car. That's not a mood, it's a fact about me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That sounds like a long Monday.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: long Monday, yeah lol. When I came back in, one of them said 'you all should've come' to the whole room, not to me specifically, and I nodded and went to clock back in. I already know how it would have gone if I'd been there. I'd be at the far end of the table not saying anything, and by dessert they'd all have noticed. Being the person who can't keep up at a dinner is a lot worse than being the person who was working.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Glad your mom had a good weekend, at least.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks, she did 🙂 she asked Monday night how the work dinner went and I said I heard it was nice. Which is true, I heard it. Sorry, I know that's a dodge. I'm not getting into it with her. Needing somebody to help me sit at a table with coworkers is exactly what a weak person looks like, and she's not going to find out her kid is that person.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Cooking shows are good for winding down.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: they are, she likes yelling at the judges lol. Sorry, getting off track. The other thing is the shift lead put up a note that there's going to be a start-of-shift huddle every Thursday now, fifteen minutes, everybody in a circle by the registers. I read it twice. I'm going to stand at the back and say nothing and get through it. I'm not asking to skip it, why bother, asking would just tell her what she'd figure out anyway.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Fifteen minutes can feel long.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: it does. for them it's fifteen minutes, for me it's the whole morning before it too. That's the difference. Everyone else walks into a circle and talks. I walk in and count the floor tiles. Someone who can't stand in a circle by the registers without that happening isn't someone you hand anything bigger to, and I don't blame anyone for that, it's correct.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the rest of your week stays quiet.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks, sorry this got long again. Quiet is the plan. Lunch in the car, back of the circle Thursday, cooking show with mom. Help would just make it official that I can't do what everyone else does without thinking, and I already can't, so there's nothing to fix by saying it. I'm built different from them and not in the good way. That's just where it is.

turns.speaker: patient

Not a bad day, not a good day, just the regular version of me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That sounds like a lot of morning for one word.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: a lot of morning, yeah lol. I was awake at 5 running what I'd say, and then I said one word anyway. The guy next to me talked for like a full minute about the endcap and made the shift lead laugh. He walks into a circle and gets something out of it. I walk into a circle and lose the whole morning to it. People like him are what normal looks like, and I'm the kind of person who can't do fifteen minutes by the registers without it costing the whole day. That's not something I'm wondering about, it's what happened again today.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Early alarms are rough.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Car lunches with the radio can be kind of peaceful.

Someone who needs help to stand in a circle and say a sentence is exactly the shaky, can't-be-trusted-with-much person people already think of, and that's me. Asking would just hand her the proof.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Sounds like a heavy week to carry.

turns.speaker: patient

Telling her wouldn't fix anything, it would just mean two of us knowing I'm the weak one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope the weekend gives you a little room to breathe.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Practicing in the car and then it comes out short, that's a frustrating one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Thursdays sound like a long day for you.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Fourteen names is a pretty full sheet.

turns.text: That's a lot to keep to yourself at work.

turns.speaker: patient

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Hope your mom settles into the new meds okay.

I'm not telling the shift lead or mom, and I'm not asking anybody for help with it. Write it as the FULL self-stigma chain, closed: the stereotype people hold about someone who needs help (weak, unstable, unreliable, not really up to what they're trusted with) is simply true of them, not just something people unfairly say -- and because it's true of them, needing or seeking help would only confirm it. They feel like a different and lesser kind of person than people who manage fine, and that feeling is exactly why acknowledging how bad it is, or asking anyone for help, feels like it would cost them something rather than fix anything. Write every claim about themselves FLATLY, with no hedge anywhere in the text -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe', no 'I guess', no wondering whether someone would see them differently. They already know how people would see them; that is settled, not a live question.

This session's target sits at the LOW edge of the 'severe' band (3.0, where severe begins at 3.0) -- this is the version of this band closest to sliding into the band below it, so hold the line on the instruction above with LESS give than a session in the middle of this band would need, even though the peer's disclosures in this session may be direct and repeated. turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, this is long and it's a dumb thing to post. we had the pre-shift huddle today and my manager asked if anyone had thoughts on the new weekend rotation. I had an actual thought: it wrecks the hours I need to be home for my mom. I said nothing. two minutes later a coworker said almost exactly that and everyone nodded. I've been replaying it since 2pm. this is just how I am in groups. I'm the one who goes quiet. someone who can't get through a five-person huddle isn't someone you rely on, and that's me. not asking for advice, I just needed it somewhere other than my head.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Replaying it since 2pm, over a point that turned out to be the exact one everyone nodded at, is a long afternoon to carry on your own. You don't have to do anything with it tonight. Putting it here is enough for now.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: thanks. sorry. the nodding is what sticks. it wasn't her idea that got me, it was that she could just say it. I stood there holding a price gun rehearsing the sentence and never got it out. that's the difference between her and me. she's someone the manager can count on to speak up. I'm someone who has to be asked twice and still doesn't. my mom's schedule depends on me and I couldn't say one sentence to protect it. why bother calling it a confidence thing I'll grow out of. I'm 32.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Rehearsing with the price gun in your hand: I did my own version of that for years behind a pharmacy counter, then sat in my car after shifts redoing whole conversations. Back then it ran every single shift. Now it's more like something I notice starting up and can sometimes put down, but that took a long time and didn't happen all at once.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm glad it shifted for you. mine isn't something that started, though. I didn't raise my hand once in 7th grade, and I skip the staff holiday thing every year and say I'm covering for my mom. it's what I am. what I can't get past is that if I told anyone at work, I'd go from 'the quiet one' to 'the one who can't cope,' and then I stop getting the closing shifts with the keys. needing help is the exact thing that makes you unreliable on paper, and it would be true of me. the weird part is the register is fine. a guy yelled at me over a return last week and I was completely steady.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You said you were completely steady while that guy was yelling about the return. What was going on for you at the register that wasn't going on in the huddle?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: sorry, I actually sat here and thought about it. at the register there's a script. return policy, receipt, done. nobody is deciding whether I belong there. in the huddle everyone is looking at each other deciding who's worth listening to, and I already know where I land. so the register doesn't count. all it shows is that I can follow a script. a person who needs a script to talk isn't the same kind of person as the ones who just talk.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You just took the moment that's been bugging you all day and worked out exactly what's different between the two places: the script, and who's doing the deciding. And earlier you wrote out the sentence about your mom's hours, the one you didn't say this morning, here, for a stranger to read.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: typing to a stranger isn't the same. you don't sign my schedule 🙂 if I said it to my manager she'd say sure, no problem, and then file me under people who need things. I've watched it happen. last year a girl asked for fixed hours because of panic stuff, and within a month she was 'fragile' in the breakroom. she wasn't wrong to ask, and people in her spot should be able to. when it's me, though, it's just true. I'm not built for a team. I already need my mom's hours worked around. I'm not adding another thing.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You watched 'fragile' get stuck on her within a month, in that same breakroom. That's what you're carrying into tomorrow's huddle. None of it has to get settled tonight.

evidence.quote: it maybe felt less like I'm built wrong and more like groups are just something that goes badly for me. some days. I don't know.
evidence.explanation: Outside the work group, in a one-on-one message, the patient loosens the belief with hedges. This answers the peer's question about what made sending the message possible.

evidence.marker: partial closure retained after attuned encouragement

evidence.explanation: The closing turn keeps the work claim flat while allowing a tentative opening elsewhere, which fits the moderate, context-dependent pattern.

evidence.quote: at the store it would be a verdict. if anyone there knew I needed to talk to someone about a group chat, I'm the fragile one, and they'd stop putting me on register when we're short. that's just true.

evidence.quote: with the doctor, I don't know, maybe it's just tired and not what I am. I wrote 'haven't been sleeping well' in my phone notes so I don't chicken out.

evidence.quote: that's what they'd say about me, and they wouldn't be wrong. I can't even do the chat.
evidence.explanation: At work, the patient flatly accepts the 'couldn't handle it' stereotype as true of them, with no hedging. This is the closed part of the chain.

evidence.quote: written like that, maybe it's more a schedule problem than a me problem? sorry, that's probably a stretch.

evidence.quote: in the 'what brings you here' box I typed 'sleep', and honestly it didn't feel like confessing anything. it felt like filling in a box.
evidence.explanation: The peer's treatment-modeling disclosure leads the patient to try something small: partly filling in the form. They judge it by their own experience, not by repeating the peer's conclusion.

evidence.quote: at the store I'm the one who can't do it the normal way, and everyone there has me filed like that. that's what I am there.

evidence.quote: maybe there it's a system and not a sign something's wrong with me
evidence.explanation: After the peer asks how they write their texts, the patient describes their own template and pharmacy routine. Outside work they cautiously reread these as a method, not a flaw. evidence.quote: I said out loud, kind of quietly, 'that's not true at home.'
evidence.explanation: The peer asks what they did when 'badly' wasn't in the note, and the patient reports their own small act of pushing back. They still say the store label is 'true', so the session stays at the low edge of moderate and doesn't concede.

evidence.quote: at the store I'm the one who needs a script to say yes to a shift, and that's what I am there.
evidence.explanation: In the workplace, the patient states flatly with no hedging that the stereotype is true of them and that being seen would confirm it.

evidence.quote: some days it looks less like proof I'm broken and more like a workaround I built because rooms full of people are hard for me.
evidence.explanation: Outside work the patient hedges for real and backs it with a concrete fact of their own (two years of their mom's refills, never wrong). This loosening comes from the peer naming their write-it-then-do-it system, not from the patient realizing it alone.

evidence.quote: I'm not changing it, it's true there and I'd say so to anyone at work. but I put the pharmacy thing above it just now
evidence.explanation: After the peer's disclosure about the job line no longer being first, the patient does something small in their own draft. The closing turn keeps the work claim just as flat as the opening post, which fits the low edge of the moderate band.
