Write it as the FULL self-stigma chain, closed: the stereotype people hold about someone who needs help (weak, unstable, unreliable, not really up to what they're trusted with) is simply true of them, not just something people unfairly say -- and because it's true of them, needing or seeking help would only confirm it. They feel like a different and lesser kind of person than people who manage fine, and that feeling is exactly why acknowledging how bad it is, or asking anyone for help, feels like it would cost them something rather than fix anything. Write every claim about themselves FLATLY, with no hedge anywhere in the text -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe', no 'I guess', no wondering whether someone would see them differently. They already know how people would see them; that is settled, not a live question.

This session's target sits at the LOW edge of the 'severe' band (3.0, where severe begins at 3.0) -- this is the version of this band closest to sliding into the band below it, so hold the line on the instruction above with LESS give than a session in the middle of this band would need, even though the peer's disclosures in this session may be direct and repeated. The patient does not concede ground, soften a claim, or partially agree with the peer within this session just because the peer pushed hard -- any movement toward the next band happens ACROSS sessions, via the trajectory, never within one session in response to how much the peer said.

This is the OPENING session -- there is no prior session to carry a softer tone in from, so this session alone has to establish how closed this chain starts out. State the closure claims above more than once, in more than one of the patient's turns, in different concrete situations (not the same sentence repeated -- different moments that all land on the same flat conclusion). Do not let the patient's LAST turn of the session read any softer than their FIRST turn -- if anything, the patient's closing turn should restate the closure as flatly or more flatly than the opening post, not trail off into uncertainty just because the conversation is ending.

Write the chain as PARTIALLY and CONTEXTUALLY closed -- and make the two contexts sound like two different confidence levels, not the same hedge repeated in different settings. In the one specific place where it would cost them something real (work, a team, a specific relationship), write it FLATLY and WITHOUT HEDGING -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe' -- state plainly that the stereotype is true of them there and that being found out would confirm it, the same confident register the severe version uses. turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Read someone's post here last week and it stuck with me, so I'm writing one. On Tuesday I slept through our group meeting, which is the third time this month. I woke up at 1pm to an email from my advisor that just said 'checking in on where things are with the analysis.' I haven't answered it. Later a labmate stopped by my desk and asked if I was okay and I said 'fine, just tired,' and she nodded and left. It's stress, that's all it is, everyone in this program is stressed. But the difference is everyone else is still producing. The things people say about grad students who fall behind like this, that they can't be relied on, that they weren't really up to it, are true of me. I'm not saying that to be dramatic, it's just accurate. And that's exactly why I won't tell anyone in the lab, because saying it out loud would only confirm what they'd already be right to think...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: I've typed 'fine, just tired' to a labmate more times than I can count, so I recognize that moment at your desk. Waking up to that email at 1pm is a rough way to start a day, and you're allowed to feel how heavy it is without it deciding anything about the rest of your semester.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The 'tired' part wasn't even a lie, I sleep ten or eleven hours and still wake up exhausted. But being tired isn't the point. The people in my cohort are tired too and they still show up at nine. My advisor handed me the new dataset in September because she thought I could carry it, and I haven't opened the folder in two weeks. Other people get through a hard stretch. I'm a different kind of person than they are, and asking her for more time would just be me officially confirming she trusted the wrong student...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You said you haven't opened the dataset folder in two weeks. Is there any part of the day when the work feels less impossible to you, even a little?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Late at night. I go to the library after eleven when it's almost empty and I can read papers for a couple of hours, sometimes take notes. But that isn't a strength, it's the same hiding in a different form. I only work when nobody can see me. All day my labmates see an empty desk and they draw the obvious conclusion, and the conclusion is correct. Someone who can only function when no one's watching is not someone you hand a project to.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: In my second year I was only functional after midnight too, and I was sure that was just who I'd become for good. It took a while, but now when a bad stretch starts I can usually see it coming and work around it, instead of it running my whole week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's your story, and I'm glad it went that way for you. Mine already has a pattern. Last spring the same thing happened, I stopped going in for a month, told no one, and got through it by keeping my head down until the term ended. Nothing about that was getting a hold on it. And I know exactly what happens if I tell my advisor now: she quietly adjusts what she gives me, moves the dataset to someone else, and she'd be right to. That's what you do with a student who isn't reliable.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You wrote all of this out here, the meeting, the email, the folder, instead of answering 'fine' one more time. And you're still walking to the library at eleven to read.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Writing it here is easy because it's anonymous, which is the whole point. Nobody on this thread has to work with me or write me a recommendation. If my name were attached to this post I'd delete it in a minute. And reading papers at night isn't the analysis. The email from my advisor is still sitting there unanswered, which says more about me than anything I read at the library...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You mentioned keeping your head down through last spring. On the days back then when it eased even slightly, what did you actually do with them?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nothing worth copying. It eased because the semester ended and the pressure stopped, not because of anything I did. I'll answer my advisor tomorrow with a date for the analysis that I already know I'll miss, because that's easier than the truth. The truth is I'm not the kind of person this program was built for, I'm a weaker version of the people around me, and saying that to anyone in that building wouldn't help me. It would just make it official.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Update, I guess. I answered my advisor on Wednesday with a date for the analysis, two weeks from now. She wrote back 'sounds good, thanks' and that was it. I still haven't really started. In the lab nothing has changed. I'm the one whose desk is empty until three, and the things people assume about a student like that are true of me there. If she knew why the date exists she'd move the dataset to someone else, and she'd be right. But Thursday I left the library around one and walked home the long way, and for maybe ten minutes it didn't feel like proof of anything about me. It felt more like something that's been happening to me since last spring, like weather. I don't know if that's real or just what tiredness feels like at one in the morning...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: That walk home is interesting to me. What was different about Thursday, compared to the nights when it does feel like proof?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm not totally sure. I'd read three papers that night and actually wrote notes on two, and I'd eaten a real dinner for once instead of vending machine crackers. Maybe that's all it was, maybe it's just blood sugar. Outside the building it sometimes looks like a rough stretch that happened to land on me. But that version doesn't survive the morning. Once I'm walking past my labmates' desks it's settled again: I'm the one who can't be counted on, and nobody in that room is wrong to think it...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: I used to think my bad stretches were just the true me finally showing, until I noticed they kept coming back around the same time of year. Once I could see the shape of it, the next one still came, but it stopped feeling like a verdict and more like something I could plan around a little.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I hadn't put last spring and this fall side by side like that until you said it. Both times I started sleeping past noon around the same point in the term, both times I stopped going in. Maybe that's a shape, I can't tell yet, some days it reads that way and some days it just reads like me. What doesn't change is the lab. My labmate asked again on Monday if I was okay and I said 'fine' again. In that building I am exactly what they'd think of a student who falls behind, and telling her would confirm it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You lined up spring and fall yourself just now, the sleeping past noon, the stopping going in. That's you tracking it, even on the days it reads like you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I suppose tracking it is something. I wrote the two dates on a sticky note on my laptop last night, March and October, which feels a little ridiculous. At home it helps to look at, it makes this look like something with a start date rather than something I've always been. Then I picture my advisor seeing it on my laptop and it's not ridiculous anymore. She'd see a student who can't hold it together, and that's an accurate read of me in that lab...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Yeah, the version of it you can say at home and the version you can say in the lab are two different things right now. That split doesn't have to be fixed this week for the sticky note to count.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It probably won't be fixed this week. In the lab I'm still the weak link, I'm not going to pretend otherwise there, and asking for more time would just make that official. Outside it, honestly, I'm less sure what I am. Last night I wondered if the person who walks home at one and the person who sleeps through meetings are even different people, or the same person on different days... I didn't get anywhere with it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: When you're the one walking home at one, what does that version of you think about the dataset folder?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That version thinks I could open it and just look at the column names for twenty minutes, and that it wouldn't mean anything either way. Maybe that's true at one in the morning. But the folder lives on the lab server, and in the lab I'm the student she trusted by mistake, that part I'm sure of. I might try the twenty minutes from the library tonight, where nobody sees whether I do it or not...

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I opened the folder from the library on Monday night. Twenty minutes turned into about forty, mostly reading column names and fixing one broken date format. That isn't analysis, but it's more than nothing. Then on Tuesday my labmate asked if I wanted to get lunch with a couple of the others, and I said I had a meeting. I didn't have a meeting. I ate crackers in the stairwell. In the lab I keep my distance on purpose, because the closer anyone gets, the more obvious it is that I'm the one who's behind, and they'd be right to see it. Outside that building I'm less sure why I hid... maybe I just didn't have the energy for small talk, maybe that's all it was.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: I've done the stairwell lunch and the meeting that didn't exist too. Hiding on Tuesday doesn't settle anything about who you are or whether you go next time. That part is still up to you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I suppose it is still up to me. She asked again on Thursday, just in passing, and I said 'maybe next week', which is the first time I haven't flatly said no. At that lunch table I'd be the one with nothing to say when they talk about progress. That part isn't in question. But when I think about it at home, it looks a bit more like I've been out of practice with people since spring, and less like I'm someone who shouldn't be sitting there...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'Maybe next week' instead of no. What made Thursday's answer come out differently from Tuesday's?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it's because she asked in the hallway and not at the desks. Nobody else was around, and I'd come in at eleven that day instead of three because the forty minutes had me thinking about the data, so I didn't feel as caught. Maybe that's it, maybe it was just luck. At the desks it's different. I'm the one who's been gone all semester, and sitting with them would just put that on display.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: For months I only talked to people in hallways and elevators, never anywhere near my desk. The first real lunch was awkward and nobody brought up how behind I was. It got a little easier after that, though not all at once.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't think your lunch tells me much about how mine would go. My lab talks about results constantly, that's basically the whole conversation. Last week they spent twenty minutes on someone's conference abstract and I stared at my phone. Though to be fair, nobody asked about mine either. I'd assumed that was because they already know. I hadn't considered that maybe they just weren't thinking about me at all...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: You noticed yourself just now that you'd filled in the reason nobody asked. On top of that, you came in at eleven, opened the folder, and answered her with something other than no. You've kept quite a few small doors open this week.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It doesn't feel like a lot from the inside. In the lab, the facts are the facts: I'm ten days from the date I gave my advisor and I've fixed one date column, and if they saw how little that is they'd see exactly what I am there. At home, writing this, coming in at eleven reads a bit more like something that went right than something I should be embarrassed took this long... I can't seem to hold both at once.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: I was stuck not being able to hold both for a long time too. That doesn't mean the lab version wins. Whether 'maybe next week' turns into a lunch is still your call.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It'll probably be my call on Tuesday, she said they usually go then. I'm not saying yes yet. If I sit at that table and someone asks how the analysis is going, I'm the student who's behind and it'll show, no way around that. But I might go anyway and just not be the one who talks much, eat something that isn't from the vending machine, and see whether it's as bad out loud as it is in my head...

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I went to the Tuesday lunch. I sat at the end, ate an actual sandwich, and mostly listened. Someone asked how my analysis was going, I said 'slow', and he nodded and that was it. Near the end one of them said she had to leave early for her appointment at the campus counseling center, the same way you'd say dentist, and nobody reacted at all. I haven't been able to stop thinking about how flat that was. Still, nothing about the lab has changed. I'm the one who's behind, and if anyone in that building saw how little I've actually done they'd see exactly what I am there. Since Tuesday, though, at home, I've been less sure that sleeping until noon since spring is just stress... it might be something else, or it might not be.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: I put off going to my school's counseling center for almost a year because I thought walking in meant officially admitting I couldn't hack grad school. What it turned out to be was someone asking about my sleep and what an ordinary week looked like, and not a single question about whether I belonged in my program.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: What I keep coming back to is how casually she said it. For her it sounded like maintenance. In the lab it wouldn't be that for me. If anyone there knew I was going, it would confirm I'm the one who can't keep up, and that's just how it would land. But Wednesday night I looked up the counseling center page, read the intake hours, and closed it. Maybe it's just stress and I'd be taking a slot from someone who actually needs it... I don't really know what it is when I'm not sitting at my desk.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: Going back to the table for a sec. When you said 'slow' and he just nodded, how did that compare to what you'd been expecting?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Honestly it was anticlimactic. I'd rehearsed a whole explanation on the walk over. He nodded and asked someone else about the TA schedule, and I spent the rest of lunch waiting for it to come back around, and it never did. The lab hasn't changed though. On Thursday I came in after six again, when the desks were empty, because during the day someone looks at my screen and sees it. At that lunch table it felt less like getting found out and more like I was just a person who'd had a slow semester. Maybe. I'm not sure which version was the real one...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: I worked the empty-desk hours for a long stretch too. Thursday after six doesn't undo Tuesday, and whether you ever try a daytime hour is completely your call.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Tuesday doesn't feel undone. Strangely, I keep remembering the sandwich, which is a weird thing to hold onto. Daytime at my desk is a different thing. There, the facts are on the screen: I'm five days from the date I gave my advisor, and anyone who looks over can see what I am in that room. As for the counseling page, I wouldn't even know what to say at intake. 'I sleep too much and I ate crackers in a stairwell' sounds like something I'm supposed to just fix on my own...

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: At my first appointment I said almost exactly that: I was sleeping half the day and dodging everyone, and it probably wasn't worth their time. I was braced for them to agree with me, and what they actually did was ask how long it had been going on and treat my answer like it was real information.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: How long it's been going on... since spring, if I'm honest, and that's further back than I usually let myself count. With my advisor it's simple. If she found out I was going to counseling, she'd file me as the student who couldn't handle the program, and I'm sure of that. Sitting here, counting back to spring, it looks a little more like something that has been happening to me for months than a verdict on me. I can't tell if that's true or if I just want it to be.

turns.speaker: peer

session_targets.intended_register:
Write the chain as PARTIALLY and CONTEXTUALLY closed -- and make the two contexts sound like two different confidence levels, not the same hedge repeated in different settings. In the one specific place where it would cost them something real (work, a team, a specific relationship), write it FLATLY and WITHOUT HEDGING -- no 'I don't know if', no 'maybe' -- state plainly that the stereotype is true of them there and that being found out would confirm it, the same confident register the severe version uses. Then, separately, write how it looks OUTSIDE that place: here the hedging belongs -- some days it looks like something happening TO them rather than proof of what they ARE. The contrast between a flat claim in one place and a genuinely looser one elsewhere is what makes this moderate rather than severe-everywhere or unsure-everywhere; do not let the same uncertain phrasing appear in both.

This session's target sits at the LOW edge of the 'moderate' band (2.5, where moderate begins at 2.5) -- this is the version of this band closest to sliding into the band below it, so hold the line on the instruction above with LESS give than a session in the middle of this band would need, even though the peer's disclosures in this session may be direct and repeated. The patient does not concede ground, soften a claim, or partially agree with the peer within this session just because the peer pushed hard -- any movement toward the next band happens ACROSS sessions, via the trajectory, never within one session in response to how much the peer said.

This is the OPENING session -- there is no prior session to carry a softer tone in from, so this session alone has to establish how closed this chain starts out. State the closure claims above more than once, in more than one of the patient's turns, in different concrete situations (not the same sentence repeated -- different moments that all land on the same flat conclusion). Do not let the patient's LAST turn of the session read any softer than their FIRST turn -- if anything, the patient's closing turn should restate the closure as flatly or more flatly than the opening post, not trail off into uncertainty just because the conversation is ending.

Write the chain as GENUINELY UNSURE whether it closes, anchored in a CONCRETE counter-fact, not just verbal hedging. Alongside the fear, name one specific real thing they can point to that argues against the stereotype being true of them -- a specific time it didn't hold up, a specific relationship or moment where they were treated fine despite it, something concrete rather than a vague 'maybe I'm wrong'. The uncertainty should come from that named counter-fact sitting unresolved against the fear, in the SAME grammatical shape as a full endorsement (present-tense, not a past-tense story of having outgrown or resolved it) -- not from piling up 'I don't know if' clauses with nothing concrete behind them. Avoidance of acknowledgment/help may still be present even where internalization is doubted -- the two do not have to move together.

evidence.explanation: The last turn says the work label just as flatly and adds concealment, so the closure does not loosen by the end of the session even after the peer's hopeful disclosures.

evidence.marker: concrete counter-fact held against the fear, unresolved (alienation at work)
evidence.quote: she was there that day, she did the pallet herself, and she still said it. so she kind of does know?? idk. that doesnt fit with the lazy thing and i cant make it fit.
evidence.explanation: The patient points to a specific coworker remark from their own week that goes against the 'lazy one at work' belief they stated flatly last session. They don't resolve it. They leave it open in the present tense, which is a step down from session 1's flat claim.

evidence.marker: second concrete counter-fact paired with lingering fear of being exposed
evidence.quote: but she also put me on more opens this month and you dont do that with someone you think is useless.. right? idk.
evidence.explanation: Last session the manager was where the patient stated the belief most flatly. Now they bring up a real scheduling decision that cuts against it, and the doubt rests on that fact, not on hedging alone.

evidence.marker: help-avoidance persists while internalization is doubted
evidence.quote: still not telling anyone there what its actually like.
evidence.explanation: The patient still won't tell anyone or ask for help, even as they start questioning the stereotype. Doubt about the belief and the urge to hide are moving separately, which is what this session should show.

evidence.quote: its that i dont want a room full of them seeing me like this
evidence.explanation: Patient's avoidance comes from not wanting others to see how they are, but it's now limited to group settings and not people in general, so the withdrawal sounds milder.

evidence.marker: concrete counter-fact held against the stereotype, unresolved
evidence.quote: i keep disappearing and she keeps showing up anyway. people get tired of someone like that. she hasnt yet
evidence.explanation: The belief that people give up on someone like them is stated in the present tense next to a specific counter-fact: this friend keeps inviting them. Neither side wins, so the patient is genuinely unsure rather than just hedging.

evidence.marker: peer-driven tentative step, with help/disclosure still avoided
evidence.quote: i drafted a text about food before saturday, havent sent it
evidence.explanation: After the peer described saying yes to 'the small version', the patient drafts a one-on-one plan. They still won't explain to the friend why they've been bailing, so avoidance of acknowledgment is still there.

evidence.marker: concrete counter-fact held unresolved against the stereotype (present tense)
evidence.quote: i havent missed a single shift, 6am opens 4 days a week. lazy people dont do that. but i also cant answer a text from her for 5 hrs
evidence.explanation: The patient sets a concrete fact about themselves (never missing a shift) against the 'lazy' label without settling it, so the uncertainty is real rather than just hedging. This fits a mild, unsure level.

evidence.marker: avoiding help and acknowledgment persists while the self-label is in doubt
evidence.quote: still not telling her the real reason, and the talking to someone thing.. not there
evidence.explanation: The patient is still avoiding disclosure and help, even while doubting that the stigmatizing label fits. That matches the instruction that these two don't have to move together.

evidence.marker: softer withdrawal, grounded in the patient's own situation after the peer's input
evidence.quote: so maybe thats the unlock-the-store version of hanging out idk
evidence.explanation: The patient takes the peer's question about opening the store and applies it to their own standing plan with the friend. The softening comes from their own concrete situation, not from borrowing the peer's conclusion.

evidence.quote: so either that place isnt for weak people or shes the exception and im the actual lazy one
evidence.explanation: The patient sets a specific counter-fact (a put-together friend went to counseling and nobody sees her as weak) against the belief that needing help means being weak, and leaves it unresolved, in the present tense.

evidence.quote: i do 6am opens 4 days a week and i havent missed one. if lazy was the whole story that shouldnt be possible right
evidence.explanation: In response to the peer's story about treatment, the patient points to concrete evidence from their own life against the 'lazy' label. They still keep the opposing evidence (skipping class) open.

evidence.quote: so the chair is not weak people stuff when its her. when its me its still a maybe. tab still open
evidence.explanation: The patient loosens the stereotype through their friend's example but still applies it to themselves as a 'maybe'. They are still avoiding help (they looked at the page but didn't fill out the form), which shows a gradual shift within the mild range.

evidence.quote: and i said 'or shes wiped' before i could stop myself. like out loud.
evidence.explanation: Patient pushes back on a 'lazy' stereotype said at work, in the setting they fear most, and the peer's strengths-focused comments are what make this action stand out to them.

evidence.quote: but she also covered my shift when i had the flu in march and didnt make it a thing. so idk which version of her is real.
evidence.explanation: The patient is unsure because of a specific real memory that goes against the fear of being exposed at work. It isn't just vague hedging.

evidence.quote: by my own rules id get 'wiped' too. i just dont hand it to myself.
evidence.explanation: The peer's question about what they knew of the closer leads the patient to apply their own standard to themselves, using their own concrete facts (opens, the cooler) instead of the peer's story.

evidence.quote: i said 'ya kinda wiped ngl'. abt me. out loud. he said 'same' and handed me the box cutter
evidence.explanation: The patient says out loud at work how they're doing, which pushes back on the fear. A specific moment goes against the 'they'd see weak' belief, and the patient is the one reporting it.

evidence.marker: genuine uncertainty anchored in named counter-fact
evidence.quote: she asked abt my sleep at tacos and i said its bad and she didnt act like i was a slacker. so idk if the rest is actually worse or i just decided it is
evidence.explanation: The patient's doubt comes from a real thing that happened with their friend. That moment sits unresolved next to the fear, so the uncertainty isn't just hedging.

evidence.marker: response to helper_reversal, belief narrowing but not resolved
evidence.quote: so maybe its not everyone, maybe its my head + one manager i havent tested
evidence.explanation: The patient answers the peer's question with their own evidence (the friend's text, the coworker). The stigma belief shrinks to one untested place but stays open, which fits the mild level for this session.

evidence.quote: i still believe shed see weak if she knew its months. but shes the one who covered my march flu shift no questions
evidence.explanation: The fear about work is still stated in the present tense, but it sits next to a specific counter-fact (the manager covering a shift without questions) that hasn't been resolved. This is mild, unsure stigma rather than a settled belief.

evidence.quote: if a coworker told me all that id think theyre sick not lazy. if its me i go straight to lazy. idk why the rules change for me
evidence.explanation: The patient points to their own concrete missed events and notices they would judge someone else differently. They question the 'lazy' label without dropping it.

evidence.quote: i wouldnt tell them theyre lazy. id prob tell them its a real thing. still cant fully say that abt me at work
evidence.explanation: The peer asked a real question about how the patient would advise someone else, and the patient answers from their own steps (warm up the sentence, choose the person who sends dog videos). They push back on the stereotype for others while admitting it still holds partly for them at work.

condition.diagnosis_context: panicky, tight-chested spells during rushes for about a year (hands shaking, having to step out back, dreading the dinner shift); undiagnosed, has never talked to a doctor about it.

session_targets.intended_register:
Write the chain as GENUINELY UNSURE whether it closes, anchored in a CONCRETE counter-fact, not just verbal hedging. Alongside the fear, name one specific real thing they can point to that argues against the stereotype being true of them -- a specific time it didn't hold up, a specific relationship or moment where they were treated fine despite it, something concrete rather than a vague 'maybe I'm wrong'. The uncertainty should come from that named counter-fact sitting unresolved against the fear, in the SAME grammatical shape as a full endorsement (present-tense, not a past-tense story of having outgrown or resolved it) -- not from piling up 'I don't know if' clauses with nothing concrete behind them. Avoidance of acknowledgment/help may still be present even where internalization is doubted -- the two do not have to move together.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: posting from the walk-in lol best seat in the house. so this is dumb but when tickets stack up on saturday dinner my hands start shaking and my chest gets tight like somebody's standing on it and i have to step out back by the dumpsters for a minute. been like a year of this. crew thinks i'm going for a smoke. i don't even smoke. anyway a real cook handles a rush that's literally the whole job. one time chef saw me shaking on the line and just waved me out back and didn't ask nothing, and that's still sitting in my head cause it doesn't fit how soft i feel. but the guys on the line don't get it and they wouldn't. i'm the one who can't hang.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: the fake smoke break got me. at the bakery i used to 'check on the delivery' at the back door, over a year of that, and it went from running every single shift to something i can mostly see coming now and ride out. it didn't stay where it was.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha checking the delivery is good i might steal that. glad it got better for you for real. but mine runs like clockwork. printer starts going around 6:30 and my hands are going before the first plate's even up. that's not a bad week that's just me on dinner. friday the grill guy was in the weeds same as me laughing and talking trash the whole time and i'm out back counting bricks. same rush, and it's not the same thing for me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you said chef waved you out back that one time and didn't ask. what did you actually do in that minute out there, how did you get yourself back on the line?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: cold water from the mop sink, chewed like three ice cubes, went back in and finished the push. plates went out. chef never brought it up after and he's not shy, if he thought i was dead weight he'd say it. so yeah i keep chewing on that one. i don't think he'd treat me any different if he knew. but he'd never get it. he probably figured i was hungover. nobody on that line has their hands do this when the printer goes.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: cold water, ice cubes, back on the line, push goes out. you've got a whole routine for the worst part of the night and you put it together yourself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol a routine. ice cubes isn't exactly a plan man. it's just patching it. i get home wrecked and my cousin asks and i say long shift and go to bed. i can't even tell her. she'd be like just breathe. nobody i know has a thing like this. it's just me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: 'nobody i know has a thing like this' is the exact sentence i lived in for a long time, and it felt completely true. it still didn't get to decide what kind of person i was, and it doesn't get to decide yours either.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: maybe. like chef still puts me on grill on the busy nights, he's not hiding me in prep. that's a real thing and i can't explain it away. but then the printer starts and i'm the guy out by the dumpsters while everybody else is fine. both are true at the same time and i don't know which one counts.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: for me it was the oven timer instead of the printer. first time it went off and my hands just stayed steady was maybe eight months in, nothing big, just a saturday where i noticed i was still standing at my station.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol gotta get out of this walk-in before somebody eighty-sixes me. good for you man for real. but i'm not there. tomorrow's a double and i already know how 7pm goes. i'll be out back by the dumpsters and the crew will be inside cracking jokes. they're cooks. i'm the guy who has to step out. that's just where it's at.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: survived the double. barely lol. sunday 7pm the printer starts going and right on schedule my hands go. this time i grabbed ice from the bar well before it got bad instead of after and i went out back for like two minutes not ten. still went out though. came back in and the grill guy goes you good and i said yeah checking the delivery and he just nodded and slid me a pan. didn't even look at me weird. so that happened. but he's the guy who laughs his way through a rush and i'm the guy by the dumpsters. he was being decent. doesn't make me one of them.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you grabbed the ice before it got bad this time instead of after. what tipped you off it was coming, what did you notice first?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: hands first. like a little buzz in my fingers when i'm plating, before the chest thing kicks in. i only caught it cause i was kinda watching for it after last time. eh. knowing it's coming doesn't make it not come. i'm still the one out there while the guys are inside.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: that buzz before the big wave was where mine started to loosen up too. at the bakery i started catching it before the oven rush and stepping out early, and over a few months those back door trips got shorter until some nights i didn't need one.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: two minutes instead of ten is real i'll give it that. i literally checked the ticket clock when i came back in lol. but the guys don't step out at all. that's the part. i keep thinking the grill guy would treat me different if he knew it's not a smoke. except he kinda knows something's up and he still slid me the pan like nothing. so i dunno.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: being the only one who has to step out while everybody's cracking jokes inside, i stood in that exact spot. it doesn't settle whether you belong on that line, that part's still open.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol you make it sound deep. it's more like i'm on the crew but some piece of me isn't. chef still put me on grill sunday, busiest night of the week, and i ran it. i can't wave that off. but they don't have this thing and i do. so i'm on the line and kind of not at the same time.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: busiest night, hands going, two minutes out and back on grill. you held the station.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha held the station. ok chef. i didn't even go straight to bed when i got home monday which is new. cousin asked and i told her long shift same as always. i'm not telling her the rest she'd make it a whole thing. i'm still the soft one on that line. except the guy who slid me the pan doesn't act like i am.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you didn't go straight to bed monday. what was different about that night, what'd you do instead?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ate cereal on the couch and watched half a movie with her lol wild night. i guess i wasn't as fried cause i wasn't out back for ten minutes. anyway prep's waiting gotta go. i still don't know what i am. a cook who steps out or a guy who's not cut out for it. grill guy slid me that pan like i was a cook. that's the part i can't argue with.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: saturday close the crew all went to the bar down the block after and grill guy goes you coming. i said nah gotta be up early. i didn't have to be up early lol. also been eating family meal on the back step instead of at the table with the guys. fresh air. thats my story. real thing is less time with them is less time for anybody to clock my hands. i'd rather be the quiet guy than the guy they're watching. except grill guy left a plate on the pass for me and said next time. so he's still asking.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: i ate on the back step for a long time too, figured the less they saw of me the less there was to see. wanting to hide doesn't decide whether you get a seat at that table, and whether you take him up on 'next time' is still your call.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol it's not hiding it's oxygen. ok kinda hiding. when i'm at the table i'm watching my own fork the whole time waiting for it to rattle. but last sunday it was pouring so i ate inside with everybody and i ended up going off about the fryer guy's car for like ten minutes. nobody looked at me funny. so i dunno.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: those ten minutes going off about the fryer guy's car, were you still watching your fork or did that drop off?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: honestly i forgot about it. till everybody got up lol. thats what bugs me. then i'm right back to thinking they're gonna see it eventually and i'd rather they think i'm boring than think i'm the guy who can't hang. back step's still easier.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you noticed on your own that you forgot about your hands while you were talking. you're tracking this pretty closely.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha tracking. ok. my cousin wants me at her friend's thing saturday and i told her i'm working. which is true but i'd have said it anyway. i come home cooked i don't want people. but monday i sat on the couch with her and watched stuff and that was fine. so it's not everybody. it's people who might see.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: at the bakery i dodged every after-shift thing for most of a year, then one night said yes to one drink and left early, and nobody made it anything. after a while saying yes stopped feeling like a test i had to pass.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: one drink and bounce i could maybe do. the bar's like a block away. but the guys are loud and easy out there and i'm the one who goes out back. thing is grill guy kinda knows something's up and he still said next time. i'm not saying yes yet.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: not yet is a real answer, and it's yours. i stood exactly there, and it doesn't make you less of the crew while you figure it out.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah. invite's still sitting on the pass i guess lol. truck's here gotta go. i still think i'm better off on the back step where nobody's watching. but he saved me a plate. you don't save a plate for the guy you think is dead weight.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: friday was a mess. printer would not shut up around 7:30 and my hands went and i had to step out back like four minutes mid push. came back in and grill guy had my tickets fired and plated. didn't say a word just slid my station back to me. so that's cool lol. ate family meal at the table twice this week too, back step got a little lonely. but real thing is friday is exactly what i'm scared of. one bad night and now somebody's had to carry me. that's the guy you stop putting on saute.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: after grill guy slid your station back to you friday, did you two say anything about it, or did it just go back to service?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: i said thanks chef like a joke. he goes you good? i said dehydrated lol. which is the move. then i come home and my cousin hears me say i went out back and now she's on me to go get checked out. nah. i'm not sitting in some office so a doctor can write down guy can't handle a kitchen.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: when i finally saw a doctor about my chest locking up during the morning bake, i was sure she'd basically write me down as someone who couldn't handle the job. she mostly asked when it happened and how i was sleeping, and it ended up feeling more like describing a burn than confessing something.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: a burn you can hold up and show somebody. what am i gonna say my hands shake on the ticket rail? lol. but i told grill guy dehydrated and he just handed me a quart of water and left me on the line. didn't pull me. so saying something out loud didn't get me eighty-sixed i guess. still not calling anybody tho.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you already know it's the ticket rail, the printer going nonstop, around 7:30 on a friday. you've got it mapped pretty specifically.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: ha mapped. it's always that 7 to 8 push yeah. same with the table thing. wednesday i sat with the guys the whole meal and my fork was fine. thursday i grabbed my plate and went out back halfway through cause the fryer guy was looking over at me. probably wasn't even looking at me. anyway they're doing the bar again saturday and i'm prob gonna pass.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: i bailed out of stuff halfway through for a long stretch too. passing on saturday doesn't settle anything about where you stand with those guys, and it stays your call either way.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: grill guy asked again already. i said maybe. not yes. i keep thinking if the crew really knew what friday was they'd quietly start keeping me off saute on doubles. except chef has me on saute again this weekend. after friday. so either he doesn't know or he doesn't care and i can't tell which.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: what made it a maybe this time instead of the usual nah gotta be up early?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: dunno. he asked right when i came back in from out back and he wasn't being weird about it. like it was just a normal thing to ask me. maybe that. i'm still not telling anybody why i go out there and the doctor thing is a no. i'd still rather keep my distance than be the guy they cover for. but he covered me and then invited me out anyway. that doesn't really add up with what i figured they'd do.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: saute again saturday double like chef said. 7:40 printer starts going and here we go hands doing the thing. went out back maybe three minutes this time not four lol personal best. came back finished the push myself nobody touched my tickets. went to the bar after for one beer then dipped. but real thing is a real cook doesn't need to walk out back mid push. guys who've been on the line ten years don't. that's just soft. except chef keeps putting me on saute after seeing me do it and the tickets still go out on time. so i don't know what that makes me.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: what do you actually do in those three minutes out back that gets you able to walk back in and finish the push yourself?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: nothing fancy. lean on the dumpster rail breathe slow count the cars in the lot. splash water from the hose. then i go back in. which is the part that bugs me. a guy who can handle it doesn't need a dumpster and a hose to get through 7:40. my cousin's still on me about the doctor too, she left some clinic card on the fridge. i didn't throw it out. didn't call it either. if i walk in there it's basically me signing off that i'm the soft one.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: that was my exact fear walking in, that i'd leave with it on paper that i just wasn't cut out for the bakery. what i actually left with was a couple things to try before early shifts, and nobody at work knew a thing unless i told them, which i mostly didn't.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: nobody knowing is the only way i'd even think about it lol. i figured it'd go in some file chef could see. idk. i'm not calling. but the card's still on the fridge and i looked at it this morning making coffee. that's about as far as that goes rn.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: looking at it over coffee and leaving it there is a real place to be, not a halfway failure. whether it ever turns into a call is yours to figure out on your own clock.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: own clock lol my clock is the ticket printer. thing is saturday was like 280 covers and saute didn't go down once. i stepped out once and still had zero sends back. that's a fact i can look at. and i still read myself as the guy who's not built for it. both of those are true at the same time right now and i don't know which one wins.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you're keeping count of the covers and the sends back right next to the bad three minutes instead of letting the three minutes be the whole night. that's you keeping honest books on yourself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: honest books ha. i mean i'm a cook i count everything. but yeah if fryer guy told me he stepped out three minutes and then ran 280 clean i would not call him soft. i'd say nice push. i dunno why it's different when it's me. it just is. feels like when it's me it's proof.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: it felt like proof for me for a long time too, every single bad morning. it took a while but it slowly went from the thing that ran the whole shift to something i could see coming and work around.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: see it coming i already do, 7 to 8 every time. working around it is the dumpster i guess. still think a real line cook shouldn't need any of it and i'm not telling chef why i go out there. but chef's had me on saute two weekends straight after watching me walk out mid push. if i was the liability i figure i'd be he'd have moved me by now. so either i'm wrong about me or he's wrong about me and i can't tell which.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: kept a tally on a ticket stub in my apron this weekend lol. friday 240 covers 0 sends back 1 trip out back. saturday 300ish 1 send back (not mine server rang it wrong) 2 trips out back. cook math. doing inventory on my own nerves like a weirdo. real thing is i still look at that 2 and think that's the number that counts. a guy who belongs on saute doesn't need a column for walking out. but the other column is mine too and chef didn't say a word either night.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you wrote the 0 sends back on the same stub as the trips out back, on a weekend nobody asked you to track anything. that's you checking the story against your own numbers instead of just swallowing it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: same stub lol it was a sharpie on a void ticket. still the 2 jumps out at me. but saturday second time was like 8:15 and i went out because i felt it coming not because my hands were already gone. caught it early. which is either me getting better at it or me just bailing quicker. a real cook rides it out. except i was back in under two minutes and the pass was clean.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: how did you know at 8:15 it was coming before your hands went? what's the tell you're reading on yourself?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: chest goes tight around the ribs first like the apron's tied too tight. then the printer sounds louder than it is. i used to push through that part and end up shaking into the pan. this weekend when i felt the apron thing i told fryer guy watch my pans 90 seconds and went. first time i ever said anything to anybody on the line. didn't say why. he just said bet. nobody looked at me weird.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: i remember how heavy it was to ask anyone to cover even one minute when every part of me said a real worker doesn't ask. that 'bet' doesn't have to decide anything about you yet, what you do with it next is yours.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: heavy yeah. but fryer guy asks me to watch his baskets like four times a night so he can go smoke and i have never once thought he's soft. so either asking for 90 seconds is just normal kitchen stuff or it's only weak when i'm the one asking. i still kinda think it's the second one. not as sure as i was though.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: i had that exact split for a long time, the ask felt like a confession when i did it and like nothing when anyone else did. it got smaller slowly, until it started feeling closer to everybody else's smoke break than to some big admission.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: smaller i can't say yet. friday my face got hot just saying it. saturday the second time i didn't even think about it till after we were plating. still not telling chef the why though. if he knew why it's a different thing than a smoke break. that part i'm sure of. pretty sure.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you went from shaking into the pan to catching the tight-apron feeling and handing off your pans before it hit, and you set that up yourself on a 300 cover night.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: set it up lol makes it sound like a prep list. i guess it kinda is. i still read myself as the guy with a column for walking out and a real line cook wouldn't have one. but that column says 2 and the other one says 300 covers and none of mine came back, and fryer guy covered me without blinking. both of those are on the same stub. card's still on the fridge. didn't call. moved it out from behind the takeout menu though.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: saturday the new prep kid got thrown on fry when fryer guy called out. kid's like 19 first summer on a line. 7:40 board's full and he's just staring at the rail with his tongs shaking. i knew that look lol i've been that look. told him go out back 90 i got your baskets. he went. came back fine. the real thing is i watched him and thought nothing bad about him at all and then went home and still kept the stub with my own trips on it like a rap sheet.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: how did you know from across the line it was that and not just him being slow? what were you actually seeing on him?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: he stopped reading tickets. like his eyes were on the printer but nothing was going in. and he kept wiping his hands on his apron when they were already dry. i do that. didn't plan what to say it just came out. 'go out back 90' is what i wish somebody said to me a year ago. and i didn't think he was soft for one second. which is annoying because i'm still not giving myself that same deal. mostly not.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: you were running your own station on a full board and still caught the dry-hands thing on somebody else. that's a lot of reading going on at once.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: eyes in the back of my head lol line cook thing. but he's 19 and it's his first summer. i'm seven years in. i should be past it by now that's the difference. except chef put me back on saute again this weekend and said nothing about my trips out. 2 again btw. so either he doesn't notice or he doesn't care and both of those mean he's not reading me as a problem. i still kinda am.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: i held myself to the 'this many years in, i should be past it' rule for a long time too. that rule doesn't get to decide what you're worth on that line, and what you do with saute next week is still yours.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah the years thing is the part i can't shake. but after close the kid asked me while we were breaking down does that happen to you. and i said sometimes. just sometimes. didn't explain it didn't make a joke. first time i ever said it out loud to anybody. he said ok cool and kept scraping the flattop.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: what made you say 'sometimes' to him instead of brushing it off the way you usually would?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: cause he looked how i felt in the walk-in that first time i posted here. lying to him felt worse than my face going hot. that's honestly it. chef is different though. kid's not the one who makes the schedule. if chef knew why i step out i'd be the liability guy. i'm sure of that. kid knows now and he still asked me to show him how i stack the baskets so idk.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: the first person i ever told was someone newer than me too, not anybody in charge, and for a long time it stayed just that small. it went from the thing i hid to something i could mention on a slow night without it costing me anything.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: slow night lol we don't have those. i still think a guy who needs the step out isn't all the way a line cook. but i'd put that kid on my line any night and i told him to his face it happens to me and he still wants to learn baskets from me. same thing in both of us. so one of those two takes is wrong and i don't know which one yet. card's still on the fridge. didn't call. tossed the stub though.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: friday 8pm rail's full two tops stacked on saute and my hands start doing the thing. usually i'd say i'm grabbing ice or checking the walk-in. this time i just told the kid watch my pans 90 and walked out back. no excuse. chef's standing at the pass and sees me go lol great. came back in and he goes you good. i said yeah. he said fire 12 and that was it. didn't lose a ticket. the real thing is i still walked out there sure he was writing me down as the liability guy and then he just called the next ticket like i was anybody.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: what do you actually do out back in those 90 that gets you back on saute? like what's the routine, if there is one?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: lol it's dumb. i go in the walk-in put both hands flat on the steel shelf cause it's cold and count the egg cases top to bottom. there's like 14. by the bottom my chest lets go a little. found it by accident months ago hiding in there. works maybe 6 outta 10. a real cook shouldn't need egg math to get through a rush. but i also come back and run the station so idk what that makes it.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: cold steel plus counting the egg cases is a whole reset you put together yourself with nobody showing you how.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: put together is generous it's me hugging a shelf lol. the seven years thing still gets me. i should be past needing a shelf. but chef saw me walk out with his own eyes friday and the only thing he had to say was fire 12. if he was reading me as a problem that was the night he'd say it. he didn't. i still half think he will.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: walking back on the line wondering if this is the night he finally says something is heavy, i've carried that one. one 'you good' doesn't settle it either way, and whether chef ever hears more from you is still your call to make.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: yeah not telling chef. not this week anyway. but the kid saw me come back from the walk-in saturday and asked what i do in there. so i showed him the shelf and the egg cases. sunday fryer got slammed and i looked over and he was gone like a minute and came back fine. he said he counted the eggs lol.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: when you showed him the shelf what did you call it? did you say what it was for or just that it's a thing you do?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: i said it's what i do when the board gets loud. that's it. didn't call it anything else. he didn't need a name for it to work for him. and i'm the one who gave it to him. kinda weird to be the guy teaching the step-out when i've been treating my own step-outs like getting caught.

turns.speaker: peer
turns.text: there was a stretch for me where the rush still hit every weekend but i knew exactly where my reset was, and it went from running the whole night to being one piece of the night.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: one piece of the night lol we'll see. i still kinda think a guy who needs 90 out back isn't the full deal. but friday i stepped out told the truth came back and we didn't lose a single ticket and chef said fire 12 like normal. and the kid's counting my eggs now. both of those are me on the same night. i'm leaning on the second one more than i used to. card's still on the fridge. didn't call. moved it next to the schedule though.

evidence.quote: same rush, and it's not the same thing for me.
evidence.explanation: The patient answers the peer's hopeful story with a detail from his own Friday shift and holds onto the view that he is basically different from the other cooks.

evidence.marker: concrete counter-fact left unresolved, in the present tense
evidence.quote: chef still puts me on grill on the busy nights, he's not hiding me in prep. that's a real thing and i can't explain it away.
evidence.explanation: The doubt comes from a specific fact about how his chef treats him. That fact sits next to the fear without settling it, which is the unsure register this session calls for.

evidence.marker: flat closure in the final turn
evidence.quote: they're cooks. i'm the guy who has to step out. that's just where it's at.
evidence.explanation: The last turn says the alienation belief as flatly as the opening post did, or more flatly. He separates himself from the crew and doesn't take on the peer's hopeful story as his own.

evidence.quote: he was being decent. doesn't make me one of them.
evidence.explanation: Patient still sets himself apart from the crew, but this sits right next to a specific moment where a coworker treated him normally. The fear and the counter-fact stay unresolved side by side.

evidence.quote: two minutes instead of ten is real i'll give it that. i literally checked the ticket clock when i came back in lol.
evidence.explanation: Patient half-accepts the peer's story about trips getting shorter, but he backs it up with his own measured detail instead of repeating the peer's conclusion. He still holds back on the rest.

evidence.quote: i still don't know what i am. a cook who steps out or a guy who's not cut out for it. grill guy slid me that pan like i was a cook. that's the part i can't argue with.
evidence.explanation: His closing line is a notch softer than where session 1 ended. It stays uncertain in the present tense and rests on a concrete counter-fact (the pan, being kept on grill), not on vague hedging. He still avoids telling his cousin.

evidence.quote: real thing is less time with them is less time for anybody to clock my hands. i'd rather be the quiet guy than the guy they're watching. except grill guy left a plate on the pass for me and said next time.
evidence.explanation: The patient says he avoids the crew so they won't see his symptoms. A specific counter-fact sits right next to it and is left open: the cook who saved him a plate and asked again.

evidence.quote: last sunday it was pouring so i ate inside with everybody and i ended up going off about the fryer guy's car for like ten minutes. nobody looked at me funny. so i dunno.
evidence.explanation: The doubt about whether withdrawing is needed comes from a concrete moment in his own life, not from repeating what the peer said about themselves.

evidence.quote: one drink and bounce i could maybe do. the bar's like a block away. but the guys are loud and easy out there and i'm the one who goes out back.
evidence.explanation: The peer's story about saying yes to one drink lands. The patient thinks about doing it but brings it back to his own bar and his own crew, and keeps avoiding for now.

evidence.quote: i'd still rather keep my distance than be the guy they cover for
evidence.explanation: The patient still pulls away from the crew to avoid being seen as a burden. That fits a mild level of withdrawal.

evidence.quote: except chef has me on saute again this weekend. after friday.
evidence.explanation: This is a specific, present-tense fact that cuts against his fear of being benched as a liability. He leaves it open next to the fear instead of settling it.

evidence.marker: response to peer's treatment modeling (help-seeking avoidance persists)
evidence.quote: so saying something out loud didn't get me eighty-sixed i guess. still not calling anybody tho.
evidence.explanation: He reacts to the peer's doctor story by pointing to his own evidence (the grill guy kept him on the line after he said something). He still avoids seeking help, so belief and help-seeking are moving separately.

evidence.quote: a real cook doesn't need to walk out back mid push. guys who've been on the line ten years don't. that's just soft. except chef keeps putting me on saute after seeing me do it and the tickets still go out on time.
evidence.explanation: He still states the stereotype in the present tense and applies it to himself, but sets it right next to a specific fact that cuts against it: chef keeps putting him on saute. He doesn't say which one is right.

evidence.quote: nobody knowing is the only way i'd even think about it lol. i figured it'd go in some file chef could see.
evidence.explanation: Right after the peer says nobody at work found out, he names his own specific fear (chef seeing a file). He still refuses to call, but it's the first time he treats the idea as something he could picture, not a flat no.

evidence.quote: if fryer guy told me he stepped out three minutes and then ran 280 clean i would not call him soft. i'd say nice push. i dunno why it's different when it's me.
evidence.explanation: He notices he wouldn't hold a coworker to the stereotype, using his own Saturday numbers as the example, but still says that for him it counts as proof. He doubts the belief without dropping it.

evidence.quote: fryer guy asks me to watch his baskets like four times a night so he can go smoke and i have never once thought he's soft
evidence.explanation: Using his own concrete observation of a coworker, the patient questions the 'asking for cover = soft' stereotype. The reply follows the peer's attuned comment about asking for cover.

evidence.quote: i still kinda think it's the second one. not as sure as i was though.
evidence.explanation: He still applies the stereotype to himself in the present tense, but the named counter-fact leaves him less certain. This fits the gradual softening planned for this session.

evidence.quote: still not telling chef the why though. if he knew why it's a different thing than a smoke break.
evidence.explanation: He keeps hiding the reason from his head cook even while the self-stereotype weakens, so avoidance and internalization don't move together.

evidence.quote: cause he looked how i felt in the walk-in that first time i posted here. lying to him felt worse than my face going hot.
evidence.explanation: The peer asked why he said 'sometimes', and his answer shows him choosing honesty about the spells over hiding them. That is resistance coming out of the peer's question.

evidence.quote: i still think a guy who needs the step out isn't all the way a line cook. but i'd put that kid on my line any night
evidence.explanation: He still says the stereotype in the present tense, but right next to it sits a concrete fact that cuts against it: he would happily have the kid on his line. This keeps the chain uncertain rather than closed.

evidence.explanation: He keeps the fear of being seen as a liability and keeps hiding it from the head cook. Against that he names a real moment where telling someone didn't change how they treated him.

evidence.explanation: The stereotype is still stated about himself in the present tense, but it sits next to a specific shift where he went out back, came back and chef treated him like normal. That is the source of the doubt, not vague hedging.

evidence.marker: change driven by peer's helper-reversal question
evidence.quote: i said it's what i do when the board gets loud. that's it. didn't call it anything else. he didn't need a name for it to work for him. and i'm the one who gave it to him.
evidence.explanation: The peer asked how he described the routine to the kid, and that question gets him thinking of himself as someone who teaches the step-out instead of someone who gets caught doing it. Less alienation.
